fields.title: Waiting on God
fields.description: Thirty-one short daily readings on a single theme: that in all our religion, personal and public, we need more of God. Murray wrote them after finding how deeply the thought met an answering hunger in others — that Christians must learn to cultivate a deeper sense of God’s presence and an entire dependence on Him. Each day takes one aspect of waiting — for supplies, for instruction, in times of darkness, patiently, quietly, continually — and turns it into prayer.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
‘Wait Thou only upon God.’

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ – Ps. 62:5

‘A God . . which worketh for him that waiteth for Him.’ – Isa. 64:4 (R.V.)

'WAIT only upon God;' my soul, be still,

And let thy God unfold His perfect will,

Thou fain would’st follow Him throughout this year,

Thou fain with listening heart His voice would’st hear,

Thou fain would’st be a passive instrument

Possessed by God, and ever Spirit-sent

Upon His service sweet—then be thou still

For only thus can He in thee fulfil

His heart’s desire. Oh, hinder not His hand

From fashioning the vessel He hath planned.

‘Be silent unto God,’ and thou shalt know

The quiet, holy calm He doth bestow

On these who wait on Him; so shalt thou bear

His promises, and His life and light e’en where

The night is darkest, and thine earthly days

Shall shew His love, and sound His glorious praise

And He will work with head unfettered, free

His high and holy purposes through thee.

First on thee must that hand of power be turned,

Till in His love’s strong fire thy dross is burned,

And thou come forth a vessel for thy Lord,

So frail and empty, yet, since He hath poured

Into thine emptiness His life, His love

Henceforth through thee the power of God shall move

And He will work for thee. Stand still and see

The victories thy God will gain for thee;

So silent, yet so irresistible,

Thy God shall do the thing impossible.

Oh, question not henceforth what thou canst do;

Thou canst do naught. But He will carry through

The work where human energy had failed

Where all thy best endeavours had availed

Thee nothing. Then, my soul, wait and be still;

Thy God shall work for thee His perfect will.

If thou will take no less, His best shall be

Thy portion now and through eternity.

FREDA HANBURY

EXTRACT

FROM

ADDRESS IN EXETER HALL

May 31st 1895

Nothing has surprised me more than the letters that have reached me from missionaries and others all over the world — devoted men and women — telling of the need they feel in their work for help towards a deeper and clearer insight into all that Christ could be to them. Let us look to God to reveal Himself among His people to a degree that very few have known. Let us expect great things from our God. At all our conventions and gatherings, too little time is given to waiting on God. Is He not willing to put things right in His own divine way? Has the life of God’s people reached the furthest limit of what God is willing to do for them? Surely not. We need to wait on Him: to set aside our experiences, however blessed they have been; our ideas of truth, however sound and scriptural they seem to us; our plans, however necessary and suitable they appear; and to give God the time and room to show us what He could do, and what He will do. God has new developments and new resources. He can do new things, things never heard of. Let us enlarge our hearts and not limit Him. ‘When Thou camest down, Thou didst terrible things we looked not for; the mountains flowed down at Thy presence.’

A. M.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
PREFACE

Before I left for England last year, I had been deeply struck by the thought that in all our religion, personal and public, we need more of God. I had felt that we needed to train our people, in their worship, to wait on God more; and that our ministry should make it a definite aim to cultivate a deeper sense of His presence, a more direct contact with Him, and an entire dependence on Him. At a ‘welcome’ breakfast in Exeter Hall I put this thought very simply, in connection with all our religious work. I have already said elsewhere how surprised I was at the response it met with. I saw that God’s Spirit had been working the same desire in many hearts.

The experiences of the past year, both personal and public, have greatly deepened this conviction. It is as if I am only now beginning to see how the deepest truth about God, and about our relationship to Him, centres in this waiting on God — and how very little our life and work have been surrounded by its spirit. The pages that follow grew out of that conviction, and out of the desire to turn the attention of all God’s people to the one great remedy for all our needs. More than half of these pieces were written on board ship, and I fear they show signs of being rather rough and hasty. Looking them over, I have almost wished I could write them again. But that I cannot do now. So I send them out with the prayer that He who loves to use what is weak may give His blessing with them.

I do not know whether I can put into a few words the chief things we need to learn. In a note on Law at the end of the book I have mentioned some of them. But what I want to say here is this: the great lack in our religion is that we do not know God. The answer to every complaint of weakness and failure, the message to every congregation or convention looking for teaching on holiness, ought simply to be: What is the matter? Have you not got God? If you really believe in God, He will put everything right. God is willing and able, by His Holy Spirit. Stop expecting the least good from yourself, or the least help from anything in man, and simply give yourself without reserve to God to work in you. He will do everything for you.

How simple this looks! And yet this is the gospel we know so little. I feel ashamed as I send out these very imperfect meditations; I can only commit them to the love of my brothers and sisters, and of our God. May He use them to draw us all to Himself, so that in practice and experience we may learn the blessed art of waiting only upon God. If only we could gain some true idea of what the influence would be of a life given wholly to waiting upon God — not in thought, or imagination, or effort, but in the power of the Holy Spirit!

With my greetings in Christ to all of God’s saints whom I have had the privilege of meeting, and no less to those I have not met, I sign myself your brother and servant,

ANDREW MURRAY.

Wellington

3rd March 1896

fields.title: The God of Our Salvation
fields.body_html:
First Day. WAITING ON GOD: The God of Our Salvation.

‘My soul waiteth only upon God [marg: is silent unto God]; from Him cometh my salvation.’ — Ps. 62:1 (R.V.).

If salvation really comes from God, and is entirely His work, just as our creation was, then it follows naturally that our first and highest duty is to wait on Him to do that work as He pleases. Waiting, then, becomes the only way to experience a full salvation — truly the only way to know God as the God of our salvation. All the difficulties people raise as the things that keep us back from full salvation have their cause in this one thing: we know too little about waiting upon God, and practise it too little. All that the Church and its members need, if the mighty power of God is to be displayed in the world, is to return to our true place — the place that belongs to us both in creation and in redemption, the place of absolute and unceasing dependence on God. Let us try to see what makes up this most blessed and necessary waiting upon God. It may help us find out why this grace is so little cultivated, and feel how infinitely desirable it is that the Church — that we ourselves — should learn its blessed secret at any cost.

The deep need for this waiting on God lies equally in the nature of man and in the nature of God. God, as Creator, formed man to be a vessel in which He could display His power and goodness. Man was not to have a fountain of life, or strength, or happiness within himself. The ever-living and only living One was, moment by moment, to give him everything he needed. Man’s glory and blessedness was not to be independent, or to depend on himself, but to depend on a God of such infinite riches and love. Man was to have the joy of receiving, every moment, out of the fullness of God. This was his blessedness as an unfallen creature.

When he fell away from God, he became even more absolutely dependent on Him. There was not the slightest hope of his recovery from his state of death except in God — in His power and mercy. It is God alone who began the work of redemption; it is God alone who continues it and carries it on, moment by moment, in each individual believer. Even in the regenerate man there is no power for good in himself. He has nothing, and can have nothing, that he does not receive each moment. Waiting on God is just as indispensable for him — and must be just as continuous and unbroken — as the breathing that keeps his natural life going.

So it is because Christians do not recognise their own absolute poverty and helplessness before God that they have no sense of their need for absolute and unceasing dependence, nor of the unspeakable blessedness of continually waiting on God. But once a believer begins to see this and agree to it — that by the Holy Spirit he must receive each moment what God works each moment — waiting on God becomes his brightest hope and joy. As he begins to grasp how God, being God, being Infinite Love, delights to share His own nature with His child as fully as He can, and how God never grows tired of taking charge of his life and strength moment by moment, he wonders that he ever thought of God as anything other than a God to be waited on all day long. God unceasingly giving and working; His child unceasingly waiting and receiving: this is the blessed life.

‘Truly my soul waiteth upon God; from Him cometh my salvation.’ First we wait on God for salvation. Then we learn that salvation exists only to bring us to God and to teach us to wait on Him. Then we discover something better still: that waiting on God is itself the highest salvation. It gives Him the glory of being All; it is the experience that He is All to us. May God teach us the blessedness of waiting on Him.

fields.title: The Keynote of Life
fields.body_html:
Second Day. WAITING ON GOD: The Keynote of Life.

‘I have waited for Thy salvation, O Lord!’ — Gen. 49:18.

It is not easy to say exactly what Jacob meant by these words, spoken in the middle of his prophecies about the future of his sons. But they certainly show that, both for himself and for them, his expectation was from God alone. It was God’s salvation he was waiting for — a salvation God had promised, and which God Himself alone could bring about. He knew that he and his sons were in God’s care. Jehovah, the Everlasting God, would show in them what His saving power is and what it does. The words point forward to that wonderful history of redemption which is not yet finished, and to the glorious future in eternity. They remind us that there is no salvation except God’s salvation, and that waiting on God for it — whether for our own experience or in wider circles — is our first duty and our true blessedness.

Let us think about ourselves, and about the unimaginably glorious salvation God has accomplished for us in Christ, and now intends to work out and perfect in us by His Spirit. Let us meditate on it until we begin to realise that every share we have in this great salvation, from moment to moment, must be the work of God Himself. God cannot hand over His grace, or goodness, or strength as something external that He gives us, the way He gives raindrops from heaven. No; He can only give it — and we can only enjoy it — as He Himself works it, directly and unceasingly. And the only reason He does not work it more effectively and continuously is that we do not let Him. We hinder Him, either by our indifference or by our self-effort, so that He cannot do what He would like to do. All that He asks of us — surrender, obedience, desire and trust — is summed up in this one word: waiting on Him, waiting for His salvation. It combines a deep sense that we are entirely helpless to produce anything divinely good by ourselves with perfect confidence that our God will do it all in His divine power.

I say again: let us meditate on the divine glory of the salvation God intends to work out in us, until we know the truth it carries. Our heart is the scene of a divine work more wonderful than Creation. We can do as little towards that work as towards creating the world — except as God works in us to will and to do. God asks only that we yield, consent and wait on Him, and He will do it all. Let us meditate and be still until we see how fitting and right and blessed it is that God alone should do everything. Then our soul will sink down of its own accord in deep humility and say: ‘I have waited for Thy salvation, O Lord.’ And the deep, blessed background to all our praying and working will be: ‘Truly my soul waiteth upon God.’

It is not hard to apply this truth to wider circles — to those we work among or pray for, to the Church of Christ around us, or throughout the world. There can be no good except what God works. Our only wisdom is to wait upon God, to have our hearts filled with faith in His working, and in that faith to pray for His mighty power to come down. Oh, that the eyes of our hearts might be opened to see God at work in ourselves and in others, and to see how blessed it is to worship and simply wait for His salvation!

Our private and public prayer are the main expression of our relationship with God, and it is chiefly in them that our waiting upon God must be practised. Our waiting may begin by quieting the busy activity of our nature and being still before God. It may bow down and seek to see God in His universal and almighty working, the only One able to work all good and always ready to do it. It may give itself up to Him in the assurance that He is working, and will work, in us. It may hold to that place of humility, stillness and surrender until God’s Spirit has brought to life the faith that He will perfect His work. If it does all this, it will indeed become the strength and joy of the soul. Life will become one deep, blessed cry: ‘I have waited for Thy salvation, O Lord.’

fields.title: The True Place of the Creature
fields.body_html:
Third Day. WAITING ON GOD: The True Place of the Creature.

‘These wait all upon Thee;

That Thou mayest give them their meat in due season.

That Thou givest unto them, they gather;

Thou openest Thine hand, they are satisfied with good.’

Ps. 104:27, 28 (R.V.).

This Psalm in praise of the Creator has been speaking of the birds and the beasts of the forest; of the young lions, and of man going out to his work; of the great sea, where there are creeping things without number, both small and great beasts. And it sums up the whole relationship of all creation to its Creator — its continuous and universal dependence on Him — in one word: ‘These all wait upon Thee!’ Creating was God’s work, and sustaining is just as much His work. The creature could no more create itself than it is left to provide for itself. The whole creation is ruled by one unchangeable law — waiting upon God!

The word simply expresses the one purpose for which the creature was brought into existence; it is the very foundation of what a creature is. God gave life to creatures for one reason: that in them He might prove and display His wisdom, power and goodness, by being their life and happiness every moment, and by pouring out on them the riches of His goodness and power, as far as each could receive it. And just as it is God’s very place and nature to be the unceasing supplier of every need in the creature, so the creature’s very place and nature is nothing but this: to wait upon God and receive from Him what He alone can give, and what He delights to give. (See note on Law, The Power of the Spirit.)

If this little book is to help us at all to appreciate what waiting on God should be to the believer — to practise it and experience its blessedness — it matters that we start at the very beginning and see how deeply reasonable this call is. We will understand that the duty is not an arbitrary command. We will see that it is not made necessary only by our sin and helplessness. It is simply and truly our restoration to our original destiny and our highest nobility — to our true place and glory as creatures blessedly dependent on the All-Glorious God.

Once our eyes are opened to this precious truth, all of Nature will become a preacher, reminding us of the relationship that was founded in creation and is now taken up in grace. As we read this Psalm and learn to see all life in Nature as continually sustained by God Himself, we will see that waiting on God is the very necessity of our being. As we think of the young lions and the ravens crying to Him, of the birds and the fish and every insect waiting on Him until He gives them their food in due season, we will see that it is the very nature and glory of God to be a God who is waited on. Every thought of what Nature is, and of what God is, will give new force to the call: ‘Wait thou only upon God.’

‘These all wait upon Thee, that thou mayest give.’ It is God who gives everything: let this faith sink deep into our hearts. Even before we fully understand all that our waiting upon God involves, and before we have been able to form the habit, let this truth enter our souls: waiting on God — unceasing and complete dependence on Him — is, in heaven and on earth, the one and only true religion. It is the one unchangeable and all-embracing expression of our true relationship to the ever-blessed One in whom we live.

Let us resolve at once that this shall be the one distinguishing mark of our life and worship: a continual, humble, trusting waiting upon God. We can be completely sure that He who made us for Himself, so that He might give Himself to us and in us, will never disappoint us. In waiting on Him we will find rest and joy and strength, and the supply of every need.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For Supplies
fields.body_html:
Fourth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For Supplies.

‘The Lord upholdeth all that fall,

And raiseth up all those that be bowed down.

The eyes of all wait upon Thee;

And Thou givest them their meat in due season.’

— Ps. 145:14, 15.

Psalm 104 is a Psalm of Creation, and the words ‘These all wait upon Thee’ were used of the animal creation. Here we have a Psalm of the Kingdom, and ‘The eyes of all wait upon Thee’ seems especially to point to the needs of God’s saints — of all who fall and those who are bowed down. What the universe and the animal creation do unconsciously, God’s people are to do with understanding and of their own free will. Man is to be the interpreter of Nature. He is to prove that there is nothing nobler or more blessed we can do with our free will than to use it in waiting upon God.

Suppose an army has been sent to march into enemy territory, and news arrives that it is not advancing. The question at once is: what is causing the delay? Very often the answer will be: ‘Waiting for supplies.’ Not all the stores of food or clothing or ammunition have arrived, and without them it dare not go on. It is no different in the Christian life. Day by day, at every step, we need our supplies from above. And nothing is more necessary than to cultivate that spirit of dependence on God and confidence in Him which refuses to go forward without the grace and strength it needs.

If someone asks whether this is any different from what we do when we pray, the answer is that there may be a great deal of praying with very little waiting on God. When we pray, we are often taken up with ourselves — with our own needs and our own efforts to present them. When we wait upon God, our first thought is of the God on whom we wait. We come into His presence and feel that we simply need to be quiet, so that He, as God, can overshadow us with Himself. God longs to reveal Himself and to fill us with Himself. Waiting on God gives Him time to come to us in His own way and in His divine power.

It is especially at the time of prayer that we should set ourselves to cultivate this spirit.

Before you pray, bow quietly before God, simply to remember and realise who He is, how near He is, and how certainly He can and will help. Just be still before Him, and let His Holy Spirit awaken and stir up in your soul the childlike attitude of absolute dependence and confident expectation. Wait upon God as a Living Being — as the Living God, who notices you and is longing to fill you with His salvation. Wait on God until you know you have met Him; then prayer will become something very different.

And while you are praying, let there be times of silence — a reverent stillness of soul in which you yield yourself to God, in case He has anything He wants to teach you or to work in you. Waiting on Him will become the most blessed part of prayer, and the blessing gained in this way will be doubly precious as the fruit of such fellowship with the Holy One. God has ordained it this way, in harmony with His holy nature and with ours: waiting on Him is to be the honour we give Him. Let us bring Him this service gladly and sincerely; He will reward it abundantly.

‘The eyes of all wait upon Thee, and Thou givest them their meat in due season.’ Dear soul, God provides in Nature for the creatures He has made: how much more will He provide in Grace for those He has redeemed! Learn to say about every need, every failure and every lack of the grace you need: I have waited too little upon God, or He would have given me in due season all I needed. And then say too —

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For Instruction
fields.body_html:
Fifth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For Instruction.

‘Shew me thy ways, O Lord; Teach me Thy paths.

Teach me Thy paths.

Lead me in Thy truth, and teach me;

For Thou art the God of my salvation;

On Thee do I wait all the day.’ — Ps. 25:4, 5.

I spoke of an army about to enter enemy territory, which, when asked the reason for the delay, answered: ‘Waiting for supplies.’ The answer might just as well have been ‘Waiting for instructions,’ or ‘Waiting for orders.’ If the last dispatch, with the commander-in-chief’s final orders, had not arrived, the army dared not move. It is the same in the Christian life: our need of waiting for instructions is as deep as our need of waiting for supplies.

See how beautifully this comes out in Psalm 25. The writer knew God’s law and loved it greatly, and meditated on it day and night. But he knew that this was not enough. He knew that to grasp the truth with true spiritual understanding, and to apply it rightly to his own particular circumstances, he needed direct teaching from God.

This psalm has always been a great favourite, because it so often expresses a deeply felt need of God’s teaching, together with a childlike confidence that the teaching will be given. Study the psalm until your heart is filled with these two thoughts: the absolute need of divine guidance, and the absolute certainty of it. And then notice that it is precisely in this connection that he says, ‘On Thee do I wait all the day.’ Waiting for guidance, waiting for instruction, all day long, is a very blessed part of waiting upon God.

The Father in heaven cares so much about His child, and longs so much for his life to be in His will and His love at every step, that He is willing to keep his guidance entirely in His own hands. He knows so well that we cannot do anything truly holy and heavenly unless He works it in us that He intends His very demands to become promises of what He will do as He watches over us and leads us all day long. Not only in special difficulties and times of confusion, but in the ordinary course of everyday life, we may count on Him to teach us His way and show us His path.

And what do we need in order to receive this guidance? One thing: waiting for instructions — waiting on God. ‘On Thee do I wait all the day.’ In our times of prayer we need to express clearly our sense of need and our faith in His help. We need to become definitely aware of how little we know of what God’s way may be, and of our need for His divine light to shine within us, if our way is to be like the sun, ‘shining more and more unto the perfect day.’ And we need to wait quietly before God in prayer until the deep, restful assurance fills us: it will be given — ‘the meek will He guide in the way.’

‘On Thee do I wait all the day.’ The special surrender to God’s guidance in our times of prayer must foster, and be followed by, the habit of looking upward ‘all the day.’ For someone with eyes, walking all day in the light of the sun is simple. Just as simple and delightful can it become, for a soul practised in waiting on God, to walk all day enjoying God’s light and leading. What we need to help us into such a life is just one thing: a real knowledge of God, and faith in Him, as the one and only source of wisdom and goodness — always ready, and longing greatly, to be everything to us that we could possibly need. Yes! This is the one thing we need. If only we saw our God in His love; if only we believed that He is waiting to be gracious, waiting to be our life and to work everything in us — how this waiting on God would become our highest joy, the natural and spontaneous response of our hearts to His great love and glory!

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For All Saints
fields.body_html:
Sixth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For All Saints.

‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed.’ — Ps. 25:3

In today’s meditation, let each of us forget ourselves and think of the great company of God’s saints throughout the world who are all waiting on Him with us. And let us all join in earnest prayer for one another: ‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed.’

Just think for a moment of the multitude of waiting people who need that prayer. How many there are — sick and weary and lonely — who feel as if their prayers are not being answered, and who sometimes begin to fear that their hope will be put to shame. Think, too, of how many servants of God — ministers or missionaries, teachers or workers of every kind — whose hopes for their work have been disappointed, and whose longing for power and blessing remains unsatisfied. And think of how many have heard of a life of rest and perfect peace, of lasting light and fellowship, of strength and victory, and cannot find the way to it. With all of these, the only problem is that they have not yet learned the secret of full waiting upon God. They simply need what we all need: the living assurance that waiting on God can never be in vain. Let us remember all who are in danger of fainting or growing weary, and let us all join in the cry, ‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed’!

If this intercession for all who wait on God becomes part of our own waiting on Him, we will be helping to bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfilling the law of Christ.

It will bring into our waiting on God that element of unselfishness and love which is the path to the highest blessing and the fullest communion with God. Love for our brothers and sisters and love for God are inseparably linked. In God, His love for His Son and His love for us are one: ‘That the love wherewith Thou hast loved Me, may be in them.’ In Christ, the Father’s love for Him and His love for us are one: ‘As the Father loved me, so have I loved you.’ In us, He asks that His love for us should become our love for one another: ‘As I have loved you, that ye love one another.’ All the love of God and of Christ is inseparably linked with love for our fellow believers. And how can we prove and cultivate this love day by day, except by praying for one another daily? Christ did not try to enjoy the Father’s love for Himself alone; He passed it all on to us. All true seeking after God and His love for ourselves will be inseparably linked with thinking of our fellow believers, and loving them, in prayer for them.

‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed.’ Twice in this psalm David speaks of his own waiting on God; here he thinks of all who wait on Him. Let this page carry the message to all God’s tested and weary ones that more people are praying for them than they know. Let it stir both them and us, as we wait, to make a point of forgetting ourselves at times, enlarging our hearts and saying to the Father, ‘These all wait upon Thee, and Thou givest them their meat in due season.’ Let it fill us all with new courage — for who is not, at times, ready to faint and grow weary? ‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed’ is a promise wrapped in a prayer: ‘They that wait on Thee shall not be ashamed’! From many, many witnesses the cry comes to everyone who needs the help — brother, sister, tested one: ‘Wait on the Lord; be of good courage, and He shall strengthen your heart; wait, I say, on the Lord. Be of good courage, and He shall strengthen your heart, all ye that wait on the Lord.’

Blessed Father! We humbly ask You: let none who wait on You be ashamed — no, not one. Some are weary, and the time of waiting seems long. Some are weak, and hardly know how to wait. And some are so tangled up in the effort of their prayers and their work that they think they can find no time to wait continually. Father, teach us all how to wait. Teach us to think of one another, and to pray for one another. Teach us to think of You, the God of all who wait. Father, let none who wait on You be ashamed. For Jesus’ sake. Amen.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: A Plea in Prayer
fields.body_html:
Seventh Day. WAITING ON GOD: A Plea in Prayer.

‘Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on Thee.’ — Ps. 25:21

For the third time in this psalm we find the word “wait”. As earlier, in verse 5 — ‘On Thee do I wait all the day’ — so here too the believing petitioner appeals to God to remember that he is waiting on Him, looking for an answer. It is a great thing for a soul not only to wait upon God, but to be so filled with the awareness that its whole spirit and position is that of someone waiting that it can say with childlike confidence: Lord, You know that I wait on You. This will prove a mighty plea in prayer, giving ever-growing boldness of expectation to claim the promise, ‘They that wait on Me shall not be ashamed’!

The prayer with which the plea is linked here is one of great importance in the spiritual life. If we draw near to God, it must be with a true heart. There must be perfect integrity — wholeheartedness — in our dealings with God. As we read in the next Psalm (26:1, 11), ‘Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my integrity,’ ‘As for me, I will walk in my integrity.’ There must be perfect uprightness, or single-heartedness, before God. As it is written, ‘His righteousness is for the upright in heart.’ The soul must know that it is allowing nothing sinful and nothing doubtful. If it is really to meet the Holy One and receive His full blessing, it must be with a heart wholly and single-mindedly given up to His will. The whole spirit that moves us as we wait must be: ‘Let integrity and uprightness’ — You see that this is how I long to come to You; You know I am looking to You to work these perfectly in me — let them ‘preserve me, for I wait on Thee.’

And if, when we first try truly to live a life of fully and always waiting on God, we begin to discover how much that perfect integrity is lacking, this will be just one of the blessings the waiting was meant to bring. A soul cannot seek close fellowship with God, or reach the abiding awareness of waiting on Him all day long, without a very honest and complete surrender to all His will.

‘For I wait on Thee’: this plea may be used not only with the prayer of our text but with every prayer. Using it often will be a great blessing to us. So let us study these words carefully until we understand everything they involve. We must be clear what we are waiting for. It may be many different things. fields.title: Strong and of Good Courage
fields.body_html:
Eighth Day. WAITING ON GOD: Strong and of Good Courage.

‘Wait on the Lord: be strong,

And let your heart take courage:

Yea, wait thou on the Lord.’ — Ps. 27:14 (R.V.)

The psalmist had just said, ‘I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.’ Had it not been for his faith in God, his heart would have failed. But in the confident assurance in God that faith gives, he urges himself — and us — to remember one thing above all: to wait upon God. ‘Wait on the Lord: be strong, and let your heart take courage: yea, wait on the Lord.’ One of the chief needs in our waiting upon God — one of the deepest secrets of its blessedness and blessing — is a quiet, confident conviction that it is not in vain. We need courage to believe that God will hear and help, and that we are waiting on a God who could never disappoint His people.

‘Be strong and of good courage.’ These words often appear in connection with some great and difficult undertaking, when a battle with powerful enemies lies ahead and all human strength is utterly insufficient. Is waiting on God such a difficult task that it too needs words like these — ‘Be strong, and let your heart take courage’? Yes, indeed. The deliverance we often have to wait for is from enemies we are powerless against. The blessings we plead for are spiritual and wholly unseen: things impossible with men — heavenly, supernatural, divine realities. Our souls are so unused to fellowship with God, and the God on whom we wait so often seems to hide Himself. We who wait are often tempted to fear that we are not waiting rightly — that our faith is too weak, that our desire is not as sincere or as earnest as it should be, that our surrender is not complete. Our hearts may well faint and fail. Amid all these causes of fear or doubt, how blessed it is to hear the voice of God: ‘Wait on the Lord! Be strong, and let your heart take courage! Yea, wait thou upon the Lord!’ Let nothing in heaven or earth or hell — let nothing — keep you from waiting on your God in full assurance that it cannot be in vain.

So the one lesson our text teaches us is this: when we set ourselves to wait on God, we should decide beforehand that we will do it with the most confident expectation that God will meet us and bless us. We should make up our minds that nothing was ever more certain than that waiting on God will bring us untold and unexpected blessing. We are so used to judging God and His work in us by what we feel that, when we begin to cultivate the practice of waiting on Him more, we are very likely to be discouraged because we do not notice any special blessing from it. The message comes to us: ‘Above everything, when you wait on God, do it in a spirit of overflowing hope. It is God in His glory, in His power, in His love, longing to bless you, that you are waiting on.’

You may say you are afraid of deceiving yourself with empty hope, because you see and feel nothing in your present condition to justify such great expectations. My answer is: it is God who is the ground for your expecting great things. Oh, do learn this lesson! You are not going to wait on yourself, to see what you feel and what changes come over you. You are going to WAIT ON GOD — to know first WHAT HE IS, and only after that what He will do. The whole duty and blessedness of waiting on God has its root in this: He is such a blessed Being, full to overflowing with goodness and power and life and joy, that we, however wretched, cannot be in contact with Him for any length of time without that life and power secretly and silently beginning to enter into us and bless us. God is Love! That is the one and only, all-sufficient ground for your expectation. Love does not seek its own; God’s love is simply His delight in giving Himself and His blessedness to His children. Come, and however weak you feel, just wait in His presence. A weak, sick invalid is carried out into the sunshine to let its warmth go through him; in the same way, come with all that is dark and cold in you into the sunshine of God’s holy, almighty love, and sit and wait there with one thought: Here I am, in the sunshine of His love. As the sun does its work in the weak one who seeks its rays, God will do His work in you. Oh, trust Him fully. ‘Wait on the Lord! Be strong, and let your heart take courage! Yea, wait on the Lord’!

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: With the Heart
fields.body_html:
Ninth Day. WAITING ON GOD: With the Heart.

‘Be strong, and let your heart take courage,

All ye that wait for the Lord.’ — Ps. 31:24 (R.V.)

The words are almost the same as in our last meditation. But I am glad to use them again to press home a much-needed lesson for all who want to learn truly and fully what waiting on God is. The lesson is this: it is with the heart that we must wait upon God. ‘Let your heart take courage.’ All our waiting depends on the state of the heart. As a man’s heart is, so is he before God. We can go no further or deeper into the holy place of God’s presence, to wait on Him there, than the Holy Spirit has prepared our heart to go. The message is: ‘Let your heart take courage, all you that wait on the Lord.’

This truth seems so simple that some may ask: Doesn’t everyone accept this? Why insist on it so particularly? Because a great many Christians have no sense of the great difference between a religion of the mind and a religion of the heart, and the first is cultivated far more diligently than the second. They do not know how infinitely greater the heart is than the mind. Here we must look for one of the chief causes of the weakness of our Christian life, and only as this is understood will waiting on God bring its full blessing.

Proverbs 3:5 may help make my meaning clear. Speaking of a life lived in the fear and favour of God, it says, ‘Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not upon your own understanding.’ In all religion we have to use these two powers. The mind has to gather knowledge from God’s word and prepare the food by which the heart and the inner life are to be nourished. But here a terrible danger comes in: that we lean on our own understanding and trust in our grasp of divine things. People imagine that if they are busy with the truth, their spiritual life will naturally be strengthened. That is by no means the case. The understanding deals with ideas and pictures of divine things, but it cannot reach the real life of the soul. That is why the command says, ‘Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not upon your own understanding.’ It is with the heart that a person believes and comes into touch with God. It is in the heart that God has given His Spirit, to be there for us the presence and power of God working in us. In all our religion it is the heart that must trust and love and worship and obey. My mind is completely powerless to create or sustain the spiritual life within me: the heart must wait on God for Him to work it in me.

It is just like our physical life. My reason may tell me what to eat and drink, and how food nourishes me. But in the actual eating and nourishing my reason can do nothing; the body has its own organs for that particular purpose. In the same way, reason may tell me what God’s word says, but it can do nothing towards feeding the soul on the bread of life. Only the heart can do this, by its faith and trust in God. A man may study the nature and effects of food or sleep; but when he wants to eat or sleep, he sets his thoughts and study aside and uses his power to eat or sleep. In the same way, whenever the Christian has studied or heard God’s word, he needs to stop his thinking, put no trust in it, and rouse his heart to open itself before God and seek living fellowship with Him.

This, then, is the blessedness of waiting upon God: I confess that all my thoughts and efforts are powerless, and I set myself to bow my heart quietly before Him in holy silence, trusting Him to renew and strengthen His own work in me. And this is exactly the lesson of our text: ‘Let your heart take courage, all you that wait on the Lord.’ Remember the difference between knowing with the mind and believing with the heart. Beware of the temptation to lean on your understanding, with its clear, strong thoughts. They only help you know what the heart must receive from God; in themselves they are only pictures and shadows. ‘Let your heart take courage, all ye that wait on the Lord.’ Present your heart to Him as that wonderful part of your spiritual nature in which God reveals Himself, and through which you can know Him. Cultivate the greatest confidence that, though you cannot see into your heart, God is working there by His Holy Spirit. Let the heart wait at times in perfect silence and quiet; in its hidden depths God will work. Be sure of this, and simply wait on Him. Continually give your whole heart, with its hidden workings, into God’s hands. He wants the heart; He takes it, and He lives in it as God. ‘Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that wait on the Lord.’

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: In Humble Fear and Hope
fields.body_html:
Tenth Day. WAITING FOR GOD: In Humble Fear and Hope.

‘Behold, the eye of the Lord is upon them that fear Him,

Upon them that hope in His mercy;

To deliver their soul from death,

And to keep them alive in famine.

Our soul hath waited for the Lord;

He is our help and our shield.

For our heart shall rejoice in Him,

Because we have trusted in His holy name.

Let thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us,

According as we wait for thee.’

— Ps. 33:18-22 (R.V.).

God’s eye is on His people; their eye is on Him. In waiting upon God, our eye, looking up to Him, meets His eye looking down on us. This is the blessedness of waiting upon God: it takes our eyes and thoughts off ourselves — even off our needs and desires — and fills us with our God. We worship Him in His glory and love, with His all-seeing eye watching over us so that He may supply our every need. Let us consider this wonderful meeting between God and His people, and take careful note of what we are taught here about those on whom God’s eye rests, and about Him on whom our eye rests.

‘The eye of the Lord is on them that fear Him, on them that hope in His mercy.’ Fear and hope are generally thought to be at odds with each other; but in the presence and worship of God they are found side by side, in perfect and beautiful harmony. This is because in God Himself all seeming contradictions are reconciled. Righteousness and peace, judgment and mercy, holiness and love, infinite power and infinite gentleness, a majesty exalted above all heaven and a condescension that bows very low — all meet and kiss each other. There is indeed a fear that has torment, and perfect love drives it out entirely. But there is a fear that is found in heaven itself. In the song of Moses and the Lamb they sing, ‘Who shall not fear Thee, O Lord, and glorify Thy name?’ And from the throne itself the voice came, ‘Praise our God, all His servants, and ye that fear Him.’ In our waiting, let us always seek ‘to fear the glorious and fearful name, The Lord thy God.’ The deeper we bow before His holiness in holy fear and adoring awe, in deep reverence and humble self-abasement — just as the angels veil their faces before the throne — the more His holiness will rest on us, and the more the soul will be made ready for God to reveal Himself. The deeper we enter into the truth ‘that no flesh glory in His presence,’ the more we will be given to see His glory. ‘The eye of the Lord is on them that fear Him.’

‘On them that hope in His mercy.’ Far from holding us back from hope, the true fear of God will stir it up and strengthen it. The lower we bow, the more deeply we feel that we have nothing to hope in but His mercy. The lower we bow, the nearer God will come, making our hearts bold to trust Him. Let every act of waiting — let our whole habit of waiting on God — be filled with overflowing hope: a hope as bright and boundless as God’s mercy. God’s fatherly kindness is such that, whatever state we come to Him in, we may confidently hope in His mercy.

Such are God’s waiting ones. And now think of the God on whom we wait. ‘The eye of the Lord is on them that fear Him, on them that hope in His mercy; to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine.’ Not to prevent the danger of death and famine — this is often needed to stir us up to wait on Him — but to deliver us and keep us alive. For the dangers are often very real and dark. The situation, whether in our earthly or our spiritual life, may seem utterly hopeless; but there is always one hope: God’s eye is on them.

That eye sees the danger. It sees, in tender love, His trembling, waiting child. It sees the moment when the heart is ready for the blessing, and it sees the way the blessing is to come. Oh, let us fear this living, mighty God and hope in His mercy. And let us say, humbly but boldly, ‘Our soul waiteth for the Lord; He is our help and our shield. Let Thy mercy be upon us, O Lord, according as we wait for Thee.’

Oh, the blessedness of waiting on such a God! A very present help in every time of trouble; a shield and defence against every danger. Children of God, will you not learn to sink down in complete helplessness and powerlessness, and in stillness to wait and see the salvation of God? In the worst spiritual famine, and when death seems to be winning, oh, wait on God. He does deliver; He does keep alive. Do not say it only when you are alone; say it to one another — the psalm speaks not of one person but of God’s people — ‘Our soul waits on the Lord: He is our help and our shield.’ Strengthen and encourage one another in the holy practice of waiting, so that each may say it not only of himself but of his brothers and sisters: ‘We have waited for Him; we will be glad and rejoice in His salvation.’

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

And now think of the God on whom we wait. ‘The eye of the Lord is on them that fear Him, on them that hope in His mercy; to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine.’ Not to prevent the danger of death and famine — this is often needed to stir us up to wait on Him — but to deliver us and keep us alive. For the dangers are often very real and dark. The situation, whether in our earthly or our spiritual life, may seem utterly hopeless; but there is always one hope: God’s eye is on them. That eye sees the danger. It sees, in tender love, His trembling, waiting child. It sees the moment when the heart is ready for the blessing, and it sees the way the blessing is to come. Oh, let us fear this living, mighty God and hope in His mercy. And let us say, humbly but boldly, ‘Our soul waiteth for the Lord; He is our help and our shield. Let Thy mercy be upon us, O Lord, according as we wait for Thee.’ Oh, the blessedness of waiting on such a God! A very present help in every time of trouble; a shield and defence against every danger. Children of God, will you not learn to sink down in complete helplessness and powerlessness, and in stillness to wait and see the salvation of God? In the worst spiritual famine, and when death seems to be winning, oh, wait on God. He does deliver; He does keep alive. Do not say it only when you are alone; say it to one another — the psalm speaks not of one person but of God’s people — ‘Our soul waits on the Lord: He is our help and our shield.’ Strengthen and encourage one another in the holy practice of waiting, so that each may say it not only of himself but of his brothers and sisters: ‘We have waited for Him; we will be glad and rejoice in His salvation.’ ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: Patiently
fields.body_html:
Eleventh Day. WAITING ON GOD: Patiently.

‘Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him.

Those that wait upon the Lord, they shall inherit the land.’ — Ps. 37:7, 9 (R.V.).

‘In patience possess your souls.’ ‘Ye have need of patience.’ ‘Let patience have its perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire.’ Words like these from the Holy Spirit show us what an important part patience plays in the Christian life and character. And there is no better place to cultivate it, or to show it, than in waiting on God. There we discover how impatient we are, and what our impatience means. We sometimes admit that we are impatient with people and circumstances that hinder us, or with ourselves and our slow progress in the Christian life. But if we truly set ourselves to wait upon God, we will find that it is with Him that we are impatient, because He does not do what we want at once, or as soon as we would like. It is in waiting upon God that our eyes are opened to believe in His wise and sovereign will, and to see that the sooner and more completely we yield ourselves absolutely to it, the more surely His blessing can come to us.

‘It is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy.’ We have as little power to increase or strengthen our spiritual life as we had to begin it. We ‘were born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of the will of God.’ In the same way, our willing and running, our desire and effort, achieve nothing; everything is ‘of God that showeth mercy.’ All the exercises of the spiritual life — our reading and praying, our willing and doing — are of very great value. But they can go no further than this: they point the way, and prepare us in humility to look to God Himself and depend on Him alone, and to wait patiently for His good time and mercy. The waiting is meant to teach us our absolute dependence on God’s mighty working, and to bring us, in perfect patience, to place ourselves at His disposal. Those who wait on the Lord will inherit the land — the promised land and its blessing. The heirs must wait; and they can afford to wait.

‘Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him.’ For ‘Rest in the Lord’ the margin gives ‘Be silent to the Lord,’ or, in the R.V., ‘Be still before the Lord.’ It is resting in the Lord — in His will, His promise, His faithfulness and His love — that makes patience easy. And resting in Him is nothing other than being silent to Him, still before Him: having our thoughts and wishes, our fears and hopes, hushed into calm and quiet in that great peace of God which passes all understanding. That peace guards our heart and mind when we are anxious about anything, because we have made our request known to Him. The rest, the silence, the stillness and the patient waiting all find their strength and joy in God Himself.

The waiting soul will come to see the necessity, the good sense and the blessedness of patience. Our patience will be seen as the counterpart of God’s patience. He longs to bless us fully far more than we can long for it. But just as the farmer waits patiently for a long time until the crop is ripe, so God bends down to our slowness and is long-suffering with us. Let us remember this, and wait patiently. Of every promise and every answer to prayer this word is true: ‘I the Lord will hasten it in its time.’

‘Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him.’ Yes — for Him. Do not seek only the help or the gift you need; seek Him; wait for Him. Give God His glory by resting in Him, by trusting Him fully, by waiting patiently for Him. This patience honours Him greatly. It leaves Him, as God on the throne, to do His work; it gives self wholly into His hands. It lets God be God. If your waiting is for some particular request, wait patiently. If your waiting is more the exercise of the spiritual life, seeking to know and to have more of God, wait patiently. Whether in shorter, set times of waiting, or as the continual habit of the soul, rest in the Lord, be still before the Lord, and wait patiently. ‘They that wait on the Lord shall inherit the land.’

fields.title: Keeping His Ways
fields.body_html:
Twelfth Day. WAITING ON GOD: Keeping His Ways.

‘Wait on the Lord, and keep His way,

And He shall exalt thee to inherit the land.’ — Ps. 37:34.

If we want to find someone we long to meet, we ask where the places and the paths are where he can be found. When we wait on God, we need to be very careful to keep His ways; outside them we can never expect to find Him. ‘Thou meetest him that rejoices and worketh righteousness; those that remember Thee in Thy ways.’ We may be sure that God is never found anywhere except in His ways — and that there, by the soul who seeks and patiently waits, He is always most surely found. ‘Wait on the Lord, and keep His ways, and He shall exalt thee.’

How close the connection is between the two parts of this command! ‘Wait on the Lord’ — that has to do with worship and the attitude of the heart. ‘And keep His ways’ — that deals with our walk and work. The outer life must be in harmony with the inner, and the inner must be the inspiration and strength for the outer. It is our God who has made His ways known in His Word to guide our conduct, and who invites us to trust Him in our hearts for His grace and help. If we do not keep His ways, our waiting on Him can bring no blessing. Surrendering to full obedience to all His will is the secret of full access to all the blessings of His fellowship.

Notice how strongly this comes out in the psalm. It speaks of the evildoer who prospers in his way, and calls on the believer not to fret. When we see people around us prosperous and happy while they abandon God’s ways, and find ourselves left in difficulty or suffering, we are in danger, first, of fretting over what seems so strange, and then of gradually giving in and looking for our own prosperity along their path. The psalm says, ‘Fret not thyself; trust in the Lord, and do good. Rest in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him; cease from anger, and forsake wrath. Depart from evil, and do good; the Lord forsakes not His saints. The righteous shall inherit the land. The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.’ And then follows — the word comes for the third time in the psalm — ‘Wait on the Lord, and keep His ways.’ Do what God asks you to do, and God will do more than you can ask Him to do.

And let no one give in to the fear, ‘I cannot keep His ways’; it is this that robs us of our confidence. It is true that you do not yet have the strength to keep all His ways. But carefully keep those for which you have already received strength. Surrender yourself willingly and trustingly to keep all God’s ways, in the strength that will come as you wait on Him. Give your whole being to God without reserve and without doubt; He will prove Himself God to you, and work in you what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ. Keep His ways as you know them in the Word. Keep His ways as nature teaches them, by always doing what seems right. Keep His ways as Providence points them out. Keep His ways as the Holy Spirit prompts. Do not think of waiting on God while you say you are unwilling to walk in His path. However weak you feel, only be willing, and He who has worked in you the willing will, by His power, work in you the doing.

‘Wait on the Lord, and keep His ways.’ It may be that our awareness of our shortcomings and sin makes this text look more like a hindrance than a help in waiting on God. Do not let it be so. Have we not said more than once that the very starting point and foundation of this waiting is utter and absolute helplessness? So why not come with every evil thing you feel in yourself — every memory of unwillingness, carelessness and unfaithfulness, and all that causes such endless self-condemnation? Put your trust in God’s almighty power, and find your deliverance in waiting on God. Your failure has come from one thing only: you tried to conquer and obey in your own strength. Come and bow before God until you learn that He is the God who alone is good, and who alone can work any good thing. Believe that in you, and in all that nature can do, there is no true power. Be content to receive from God, moment by moment, the working of His mighty grace and life within you. Then waiting on God will become the renewing of your strength to run in His ways and not be weary, to walk in His paths and never faint. ‘Wait on the Lord, and keep His ways’ will be command and promise in one.

fields.title: For More Than We Know
fields.body_html:
Thirteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For More than We Know.

‘And now, Lord, what wait I for? My hope is in Thee. Deliver me from all my transgressions.’ — Ps. 39:7, 8.

There may be times when we feel as if we do not know what we are waiting for. There may be other times when we think we do know — and when it would be very good for us to realise that we do not know what we ought to ask for. God is able to do for us exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, and we are in danger of limiting Him when we confine our desires and prayers to our own ideas of them. It is a great thing at times to say, as our psalm says, ‘And now, Lord, what wait I for?’ I hardly know or can say; this alone I can say — ‘My hope is in Thee.’

How clearly we see this limiting of God in the case of Israel! When Moses promised them meat in the wilderness, they doubted, saying, ‘Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? He smote the rock that the water gushed out; can He give bread also? Can He provide flesh for His people?’ If they had been asked whether God could provide streams in the desert, they would have said yes. God had done it, and He could do it again. But when it came to the thought of God doing something new, they limited Him. Their expectation could not rise above their past experience, or above their own ideas of what was possible. In the same way, we may be limiting God by our own ideas of what He has promised or is able to do. Let us beware of limiting the Holy One of Israel in our very prayers. Let us believe that every promise of God we plead has a divine meaning, infinitely beyond our thoughts about it. Let us believe that His fulfilment of it can come with a power and an abundance of grace beyond the widest reach of our thinking. And so let us cultivate the habit of waiting on God, not only for what we think we need, but for all that His grace and power are ready to do for us.

In every true prayer two hearts are at work. One is your heart, with its small, dark, human thoughts of what you need and what God can do. The other is God’s great heart, with its infinite, divine purposes of blessing. What do you think? Which of the two should have the larger place as you come to Him? Without doubt, the heart of God: everything depends on knowing it and being taken up with it. But how seldom this happens! This is what waiting on God is meant to teach you. Just think of God’s wonderful love and redemption, and of the meaning these words must have for Him. Confess how little you understand what God is willing to do for you, and each time you pray, say, ‘And now, what wait I for?’ My heart cannot say. God’s heart knows, and is waiting to give. ‘My hope is in Thee.’ Wait on God to do for you more than you can ask or think.

Apply this to the prayer that follows: ‘Deliver me from all my transgressions.’ You have prayed to be delivered from bad temper, or pride, or self-will, and it seems to be in vain. Could it be that you have had your own ideas about how far and in what way God would do it, and have never waited on the God of glory to do for you, according to the riches of His glory, what has never entered the heart of man to imagine? Learn to worship God as the God who does wonders, who wants to prove in you that He can do something supernatural and divine. Bow before Him, wait on Him, until your soul realises that you are in the hands of a divine and almighty worker. Be willing not to know what He will do, or how; expect it to be something altogether God-like — something to be waited for in deep humility and received only by His divine power. Let ‘And now, Lord, what wait I for? My hope is in Thee’ become the spirit of every longing and every prayer. In His time He will do His work.

Dear soul, as you wait on God you may often be close to growing weary, because you hardly know what to expect. I urge you, take courage — this not-knowing is often one of the best signs. He is teaching you to leave everything in His hands and to wait on Him alone. ‘Wait on the Lord! Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yea, wait on the Lord.’

fields.title: The Way to the New Song
fields.body_html:
Fourteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: The Way to the New Song.

‘I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined unto me, and heard my cry. . . . And He hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God.’ — Ps. 40:1-3.

Come and listen to the testimony of someone who can speak from experience of the sure and blessed outcome of waiting patiently on God. True patience is so foreign to our self-confident nature, so indispensable in our waiting upon God, and so essential a part of true faith, that we may well meditate once again on what the word has to teach us.

The word “patience” comes from the Latin word for suffering. It suggests being held under the pressure of some power we want to be free from. At first we submit against our will; then experience teaches us that when resisting is useless, patient endurance is the wisest course. In waiting on God it is of infinite importance that we submit not merely because we are forced to, but because we lovingly and joyfully agree to be in the hands of our blessed Father. Then patience becomes our highest blessedness and our highest grace. It honours God and gives Him time to have His way with us. It is the highest expression of our faith in His goodness and faithfulness. It brings the soul perfect rest in the assurance that God is carrying on His work. It is the sign of our full consent that God should deal with us in whatever way and at whatever time He thinks best. True patience is the losing of our self-will in His perfect will.

This kind of patience is needed for true and full waiting on God. Such patience is the growth and fruit of our first lessons in the school of waiting. Many people will find it strange how difficult it is truly to wait upon God. There is the great stillness of soul before God that sinks into its own helplessness and waits for Him to reveal Himself; the deep humility that is afraid to let its own will or strength do anything except as God works in it to will and to do; the meekness that is content to be nothing and know nothing except as God gives His light; the complete surrender of the will that only wants to be a vessel in which His holy will can move and shape. None of these elements of perfect patience is found all at once. But they will come, in measure, as the soul holds its position and says again and again: ‘Truly my soul waiteth upon God; from Him cometh my salvation: He only is my rock and my salvation.’

Have you ever noticed the proof we have, in these words of Paul, that patience is a grace for which very special grace is given? ‘Strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power, unto all’ — what? ‘patience and long-suffering with joyfulness.’ Yes, if we are to wait on God in all patience, we need to be strengthened with all of God’s might, and that in proportion to His glorious power. It is God revealing Himself in us as our life and strength who will enable us to leave everything in His hands with perfect patience. If anyone is inclined to lose heart because they do not have such patience, let them take courage. It is in the course of our weak and very imperfect waiting that God Himself, by His hidden power, strengthens us and works out in us the patience of the saints — the patience of Christ Himself.

Listen to the voice of someone who was deeply tested: ‘I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined unto me, and heard my cry.’ Hear what he went through: ‘He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings. And He has put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God.’ Waiting patiently on God brings a rich reward. The deliverance is sure; God Himself will put a new song into your mouth. O soul, do not be impatient! It may be in the exercise of prayer and worship that you find it hard to wait; or in the delay over definite requests; or in the fulfilment of your heart’s desire for God to reveal Himself in a deeper spiritual life. Whatever it is, do not be afraid, but rest in the Lord and wait patiently for Him. And if you sometimes feel as though patience is not your gift, then remember that it is God’s gift, and take up that prayer (2 Thess. 3:5 R.V.): ‘The Lord direct your hearts into the patience of Christ.’ He Himself will guide you into the patience with which you are to wait on God.

It is the highest expression of our faith in His goodness and faithfulness. It brings the soul perfect rest in the assurance that God is carrying on His work. It is the sign of our full consent that God should deal with us in whatever way and at whatever time He thinks best. True patience is the losing of our self-will in His perfect will. Many people will find it strange how difficult it is truly to wait upon God. None of these elements of perfect patience is found all at once. But they will come, in measure, as the soul holds its position and says again and again: ‘Truly my soul waiteth upon God; from Him cometh my salvation: He only is my rock and my salvation.’ Have you ever noticed the proof we have, in these words of Paul, that patience is a grace for which very special grace is given? ‘Strengthened with all might, according to His glorious power, unto all’ — what? ‘patience and long-suffering with joyfulness.’ Yes, if we are to wait on God in all patience, we need to be strengthened with all of God’s might, and that in proportion to His glorious power. It is God revealing Himself in us as our life and strength who will enable us to leave everything in His hands with perfect patience. If anyone is inclined to lose heart because they do not have such patience, let them take courage. It is in the course of our weak and very imperfect waiting that God Himself, by His hidden power, strengthens us and works out in us the patience of the saints — the patience of Christ Himself. Listen to the voice of someone who was deeply tested: ‘I waited patiently for the Lord, and He inclined unto me, and heard my cry.’ Hear what he went through: ‘He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings. And He has put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God.’ Waiting patiently on God brings a rich reward. The deliverance is sure; God Himself will put a new song into your mouth. O soul, do not be impatient! It may be in the exercise of prayer and worship that you find it hard to wait; or in the delay over definite requests; or in the fulfilment of your heart’s desire for God to reveal Himself in a deeper spiritual life. Whatever it is, do not be afraid, but rest in the Lord and wait patiently for Him. And if you sometimes feel as though patience is not your gift, then remember that it is God’s gift, and take up that prayer (2 Thess. 3:5 R.V.): ‘The Lord direct your hearts into the patience of Christ.’ He Himself will guide you into the patience with which you are to wait on God. ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For His Counsel
fields.body_html:
Fifteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For His Counsel.

‘They soon forgot His works: they waited not for His counsel.’ — Ps. 106:13.

This is said of the sin of God’s people in the wilderness. He had redeemed them wonderfully, and was ready to supply their every need just as wonderfully. But when the time of need came, ‘they waited not for His counsel.’ They did not remember that Almighty God was their Leader and Provider; they did not ask what His plans might be. They simply followed the thoughts of their own hearts, and tested and provoked God by their unbelief. ‘They waited not for His counsel.’

How this has been the sin of God’s people in every age! In the land of Canaan, in Joshua’s day, the only three failures we read of all came from this one sin. In going up against Ai, in making a covenant with the Gibeonites, and in settling down without going up to possess the whole land, they did not wait for His counsel. And so even the mature believer is in danger from this most subtle of temptations: taking God’s words and forming his own ideas about them, instead of waiting for His counsel. Let us take the warning and see what Israel teaches us. And let us especially regard it not only as a danger to which the individual is exposed, but as one that God’s people, as a body, need to guard against.

Our whole relationship with God is rooted in this: His will is to be done in us and through us as it is in heaven. He has promised to make His will known to us by His Spirit, the Guide into all truth. And our position is to be one of waiting for His counsel as the only guide of our thoughts and actions. In our church worship, in our prayer meetings, in our conventions, in all our meetings as managers or directors or committees or helpers in any part of God’s work, our first aim should always be to find out the mind of God. God always works according to the counsel of His will. The more that counsel is sought and found and honoured, the more surely and mightily God will do His work for us and through us.

The great danger in all such gatherings is that, aware that we have our Bible, our past experience of God’s leading, our sound creed and our honest wish to do God’s will, we trust in these things, and do not realise that at every step we need — and may have — heavenly guidance. There may be aspects of God’s will, applications of God’s word, experiences of God’s close presence and leading, and displays of the power of His Spirit, of which we as yet know nothing. God may be willing — no, God is willing — to open these up to souls who are firmly set on letting Him have His way entirely, and who are willing to wait patiently for Him to make it known. When we come together to praise God for all He has done and taught and given, we may at the same time be limiting Him by not expecting greater things. It was after God had given them water from the rock that they did not trust Him for bread. It was after God had given Jericho into his hands that Joshua thought victory over Ai was certain; he now knew what God could do, and did not wait for counsel from God. And so, while we think we know and trust God’s power for what we may expect, we may be hindering Him by not giving Him time, and by not deliberately cultivating the habit of waiting for His counsel.

A minister has no more solemn duty than teaching people to wait upon God. Why was it that in the house of Cornelius, ‘Peter spoke these words, the Holy Ghost fell upon all that heard him’? They had said, ‘We are here before God to hear all things that are commanded you of God.’ We may come together to give and to hear the most earnest exposition of God’s truth and gain little spiritual profit, if there is no waiting for God’s counsel. In all our gatherings we need to believe in the Holy Spirit as the Guide and Teacher of God’s saints when they wait to be led by Him into the things that God has prepared and that the heart cannot imagine.

More stillness of soul to realise God’s presence; more awareness of how little we know of what God’s great plans may be; more faith in the certainty that God has greater things to show us; more longing that He Himself may be revealed in new glory: these must be the marks of the gatherings of God’s saints, if they want to escape the reproach, ‘They waited not for His counsel.’

fields.title: For His Light in the Heart
fields.body_html:
Sixteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For His Light in the Heart.

‘I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait,

And in His word do I hope.

My soul waiteth for the Lord

more than they that watch for the morning:

More than they that watch for the morning.’ — Ps. 130:5, 6.

With what intense longing the morning light is often waited for! By sailors on a wrecked ship; by a traveller lost in the dark in a dangerous country; by an army that finds itself surrounded by the enemy. The morning light will show what hope of escape there may be. The morning may bring life and freedom. In the same way, God’s saints in darkness have longed for the light of His face more than watchmen long for the morning. They have said, ‘More than watchmen for the morning, my soul waiteth for the Lord.’ Can we say that too? Our waiting on God can have no higher aim than simply to have His light shine on us, in us and through us all day long.

God is Light. God is a Sun. Paul says: ‘God has shined in our hearts to give the light.’ What light? ‘The light of the glory of God, in the face of Jesus Christ.’ Just as the sun pours its beautiful, life-giving light on and into our earth, so God shines into our hearts the light of His glory and His love in Christ His Son. Our heart is meant to have that light filling it and gladdening it all day long. It can have it, because God is our sun, and it is written, ‘Your sun shall no more go down forever.’ God’s love shines on us without ceasing.

But can we really enjoy it all day long? We can. And how? Let nature give us the answer. Those beautiful trees and flowers, and all this green grass — what do they do to keep the sun shining on them? Nothing; they simply bask in the sunshine when it comes. The sun is millions of miles away, yet across all that distance it sends its own light and joy, and the tiniest flower that lifts its little head upward is met by the same overflowing light and blessing that floods the widest landscape. We do not have to worry about the light we need for our day’s work. The sun takes care of that; it provides the light and shines it all around us all day long. We simply count on it, receive it and enjoy it.

The only difference between nature and grace is this: what the trees and flowers do unconsciously as they drink in the blessing of the light, we are to do as a willing and loving acceptance. Faith — simple faith in God’s word and love — is to be the opening of our eyes and of our hearts to receive and enjoy the unspeakable glory of His grace. And just as the trees, day after day and month after month, stand and grow into beauty and fruitfulness simply by welcoming whatever sunshine the sun may give, so the very highest exercise of our Christian life is simply to abide in the light of God, and let it — let Him — fill us with the life and brightness it brings.

And perhaps you ask: Can it really be that I can rejoice in God’s light all day as naturally and heartily as I notice and enjoy the beauty of a bright, sunny morning? It can indeed. From my breakfast table I look out on a beautiful valley, with trees and vineyards and mountains. In our spring and autumn months the morning light is exquisite, and almost without thinking we say, How beautiful! And the question comes: Is it only the light of the sun that is to bring such continual beauty and joy? Has no provision been made for the light of God to be just as unceasing a source of joy and gladness? Indeed it has — if only the soul will be still and wait on Him, and simply let God shine.

Dear soul, learn to wait on the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning. Everything within you may be very dark; is that not the very best reason for waiting for the light of God? The first glimmers of light may only be enough to show up the darkness and to humble you painfully because of sin. Can you not trust the light to drive out the darkness? Do believe that it will. Just bow, even now, in stillness before God, and wait on Him to shine into you. Say in humble faith: God is light — infinitely brighter and more beautiful than the light of the sun. God is light: the Father, the eternal, unapproachable and incomprehensible light; the Son, the light concentrated, embodied and revealed; the Spirit, the light entering, dwelling and shining in our hearts. God is light, and He is shining here on my heart. I have been so taken up with the feeble candles of my own thoughts and efforts that I have never opened the shutters to let His light in. Unbelief has kept it out. I bow in faith: God’s light is shining into my heart. The God of whom Paul wrote, ‘God hath shined into our heart,’ is my God. What would I think of a sun that could not shine? What shall I think of a God who does not shine? No — God shines! God is light! I will take time, and simply be still, and rest in the light of God. My eyes are weak and the windows are not clean, but I will wait on the Lord. The light does shine; the light will shine in me and make me full of light. And I will learn to walk all day long in the light and joy of God. My soul waits on the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning.
