fields.title: In Times of Darkness
fields.body_html:
Seventeenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: In Times of Darkness.

‘I will wait upon the Lord, that hideth His face from the house of Jacob; and I will look for Him.’ — Isa. 8:17.

Here we have a servant of God waiting on Him not for himself but for his people, from whom God was hiding His face. It suggests to us that our waiting upon God, though it begins with our personal needs — with the desire for God to reveal Himself, or for answers to our own requests — need not and must not stop there. We may be walking in the full light of God’s face while God is still hiding His face from His people around us. Far from being content to think that this is nothing but the just punishment for their sin, or the result of their indifference, we are called to think with tender hearts of their sad condition, and to wait on God on their behalf. The privilege of waiting upon God brings great responsibility. When Christ entered God’s presence, He at once used His place of privilege and honour as intercessor. In the same way, if we know what it really is to enter in and wait upon God, we must use our access for our less favoured brothers and sisters. ‘I will wait upon the Lord, who hides His face from the house of Jacob.’

You worship with a particular congregation. Perhaps there is not the spiritual life or joy, in either the preaching or the fellowship, that you would like. You belong to a Church with its many congregations. There is so much error and worldliness, so much seeking after human wisdom and culture, so much trust in ordinances and ceremonies, that you are not surprised that God hides His face in many places, and that there is so little power for conversion or true building up. Then there are branches of Christian work you are connected with — a Sunday school, a gospel hall, a young men’s association, a mission overseas — in which the weakness of the Spirit’s working seems to show that God is hiding His face. You think you know the reason, too. There is too much trust in people and money; too much formality and self-indulgence; too little faith and prayer; too little love and humility; too little of the spirit of the crucified Jesus. At times you feel that things are hopeless, that nothing will help.

Do believe that God can help, and will help. Let the spirit of the prophet come into you as you take up his words, and set yourself to wait on God on behalf of His wandering children. Instead of taking a tone of judgment or condemnation, of discouragement or despair, realise your calling to wait upon God. If others fail to do it, give yourself to it twice as much. The deeper the darkness, the greater the need to appeal to the one and only Deliverer. The greater the self-confidence around you that does not know it is poor and wretched and blind, the more urgent the call on you — who claim to see the evil and to have access to Him who alone can help — to be at your post, waiting upon God. Whenever you are tempted to complain or to sigh, say again and again: ‘I will wait on the Lord, who hides His face from the house of Jacob.’

There is a still larger circle: the Christian Church throughout the world. Think of the Greek, Roman Catholic and Protestant churches, and the condition of the millions who belong to them. Or think only of the Protestant churches, with their open Bible and orthodox creeds. How much nominal profession and formality there is! How much of the rule of the flesh and of man in the very temple of God! And what abundant proof that God does hide His face!

What are those who see and mourn this to do? The first thing to do is this: ‘I will wait on the Lord, who hides His face from the house of Jacob.’ Let us wait on God in humble confession of the sins of His people. Let us take time to wait on Him in this. Let us wait on God in tender, loving intercession for all the saints, our beloved brothers and sisters, however wrong their lives or their teaching may seem. Let us wait on God in faith and expectation until He shows us that He will hear. Let us wait on God, simply offering ourselves to Him, and earnestly praying that He would send us to our brothers and sisters. Let us wait on God and give Him no rest until He makes Zion a joy in the earth. Yes, let us rest in the Lord and wait patiently for Him who now hides His face from so many of His children. And as we long for Him to lift up the light of His face on all His people, let us say, ‘I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and my hope is in His word. My soul waits for the Lord, more than the watchers for the morning, the watchers for the morning.’

fields.title: To Reveal Himself
fields.body_html:
Eighteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: To Reveal Himself.

‘And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He will save us: THIS IS THE LORD; we have waited for Him, we will rejoice and be glad in His salvation.’ — Isa. 25:9.

In this passage we find two precious thoughts.

The first is that these are the words of God’s people who have been waiting on Him together. The second is that the fruit of their waiting has been that God has revealed Himself so clearly that they could joyfully say, Lo, this is our God: this is the Lord. What we need to learn is the power and blessing of waiting together.

Notice the words repeated twice: ‘We have waited for Him.’ In some time of trouble the hearts of the people had been drawn together. Giving up all human hope or help, they had set themselves with one heart to wait for their God. Is this not exactly what we need in our churches and conventions and prayer meetings? Is the need of the Church and the world not great enough to demand it? Are there not evils in the Church of Christ that no human wisdom can deal with? Do we not have ritualism and rationalism, formalism and worldliness, robbing the Church of its power? Do we not have culture and money and pleasure threatening its spiritual life? Are the Church’s resources not utterly inadequate to face the forces of unbelief and wickedness and misery in Christian countries and in the heathen world? And has not provision been made, in God’s promise and in the power of the Holy Spirit, that can meet the need and give the Church the restful assurance that she is doing all that her God expects of her? And would not waiting on God together for the supply of His Spirit surely be the blessing we need? We cannot doubt it.

The aim of a more definite waiting upon God in our gatherings would be very much the same as in personal worship. fields.title: As a God of Judgment
fields.body_html:
Nineteenth Day. WAITING ON GOD: As a God of Judgment.

‘Yea, in the way of Thy judgments, O Lord, have we waited for Thee: . . . for when Thy judgments are on the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.’ — Isa. 26:8, 9.

‘The Lord is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for Him.’ — Isa. 30:18.

God is a God of mercy and a God of judgment. Mercy and judgment always go together in His dealings. In the flood, in the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, in the overthrow of the Canaanites, we always see mercy in the midst of judgment. We see it, too, within the inner circle of His own people: judgment punishes the sin, while mercy saves the sinner. Or rather, mercy saves the sinner not in spite of, but by means of, the very judgment that fell on his sin. As we wait on God we must be careful not to forget this: as we wait, we must expect Him as a God of judgment.

‘In the way of Thy judgments, have we waited for Thee.’ This will prove true in our inner experience. If we are honest in our longing for holiness, and in our prayer to be wholly the Lord’s, His holy presence will stir up and expose hidden sin. It will bring us very low in the bitter conviction of the evil of our nature — its opposition to God’s law, and its powerlessness to fulfil that law. The words will come true: ‘Who may abide the day of His coming, for HE is like a refiner’s fire.’ ‘O that Thou would come down, as when the melting fire burns!’ In great mercy God carries out His judgments on sin within the soul, as He makes it feel its wickedness and guilt. Many try to run from these judgments; but the soul that longs for God, and for deliverance from sin, bows under them in humility and hope. In the silence of the soul it says, ‘Arise, O Lord! and let Thine enemies be scattered. In the way of Thy judgments we have waited for Thee.’

No one who is trying to learn the blessed art of waiting on God should be surprised if, at first, the attempt to wait on Him only uncovers more of their sin and darkness. No one should despair because unconquered sins, or evil thoughts, or great darkness seem to hide God’s face. In His own beloved Son on Calvary — the gift and bearer of His mercy — was the mercy not, as it were, hidden and lost in the judgment? Oh, submit, and sink down deep under the judgment of every sin of yours: judgment prepares the way, and breaks out into wonderful mercy. It is written, ‘Thou shalt be redeemed with judgment.’ Wait on God in the faith that His tender mercy is working out your redemption in you, in the midst of judgment. Wait for Him; He will be gracious to you.

There is another application still, one of unspeakable solemnity. We are expecting God to visit this earth in the way of His judgments; we are waiting for Him. What a thought! We know about these coming judgments. We know that there are tens of thousands of professing Christians among us who go on living carelessly, and who, if no change comes, must perish under God’s hand. Oh, shall we not do our utmost to warn them, to plead with them and for them, in the hope that God may have mercy on them? If we feel our lack of boldness, lack of zeal, lack of power, shall we not begin to wait on God more definitely and persistently as a God of judgment? Let us ask Him to reveal Himself in the judgments coming on our very own friends in such a way that we are filled with a new fear of Him and for them, and compelled to speak and pray as never before. Truly, waiting on God is not meant to be a spiritual self-indulgence. Its aim is to let God and His holiness, Christ and the love that died on Calvary, the Spirit and the fire that burns in heaven and came down to earth, take possession of us — so that we warn and rouse people with the message that we are waiting for God in the way of His judgments. O Christian, prove that you really believe in the God of judgment!

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: Who Waits on Us
fields.body_html:
Twentieth Day. WAITING ON GOD: Who Waits on Us.

‘And therefore will the Lord wait, that He may be gracious unto you; and therefore will He be exalted, that He may have mercy upon you: for the Lord is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for Him.’ — Isa. 30:18

We must think not only of our waiting upon God, but of something more wonderful still: God’s waiting upon us. Seeing Him waiting on us will give new energy and inspiration to our waiting on Him. It will give us an unspeakable confidence that our waiting cannot be in vain. If He is waiting for us, then we may be sure that we are more than welcome — that He rejoices to find those He has been looking for. Let us try even now, at this very moment, in a spirit of humble waiting on God, to discover something of what this means: ‘Therefore will the Lord wait, that He may be gracious unto you.’ We will accept the message and echo it back: ‘Blessed are all they that wait for Him.’

Look up and see the great God on His throne. He is Love — an unceasing and inexpressible desire to share His own goodness and blessedness with all His creatures. He longs to bless, and delights in it. He has unimaginably glorious purposes for every one of His children: to reveal His love and power in them by the power of His Holy Spirit. He waits with all the longing of a father’s heart. He waits so that He may be gracious to you. And every time you come to wait on Him, or try to keep up the holy habit of waiting in daily life, you may look up and see Him ready to meet you, waiting so that He may be gracious to you. Yes, link every act, every breath, of the life of waiting with faith’s vision of your God waiting for you.

And you may ask: If He waits to be gracious, why is it that even after I come and wait on Him, He does not give the help I am looking for, but waits on, longer and longer? There is a twofold answer. The first is this: God is a wise farmer, ‘who waits for the precious fruit of the earth, and has long patience for it.’ He cannot gather the fruit until it is ripe. He knows when we are spiritually ready to receive the blessing, for our good and His glory. Waiting in the sunshine of His love is what will ripen the soul for His blessing. Waiting under the cloud of trial, which breaks in showers of blessing, is just as necessary. Be assured that if God waits longer than you would like, it is only to make the blessing doubly precious. God waited four thousand years, until the fullness of time, before He sent His Son. Our times are in His hands. He will avenge His elect speedily. He will hurry to help us, and not delay one hour too long.

The second answer points back to what has been said before. The Giver is more than the gift; God is more than the blessing; and being kept waiting on Him is the only way we learn to find our life and joy in Him. Oh, if God’s children only knew what a glorious God they have, and what a privilege it is to be joined in fellowship with Him, they would rejoice in Him even when He keeps them waiting. They would come to understand better than ever: ‘Therefore will the Lord wait, that He may be gracious unto you.’ His waiting will be the highest proof of His graciousness.

‘Blessed are all they that wait for Him.’ Our queen has her ladies-in-waiting. The position is one of subordination and service, yet it is regarded as one of the highest dignity and privilege, because a wise and gracious sovereign makes them her companions and friends. What dignity and blessedness it is to be attendants-in-waiting on the Everlasting God — always on the watch for every sign of His will or favour, always aware of His nearness, His goodness and His grace! ‘The Lord is good to them that wait for Him.’ ‘Blessed are all they that wait for Him.’ Yes, it is a blessed thing when a waiting soul and a waiting God meet each other. God cannot do His work unless He waits, and we wait, for His time. Let waiting be our work, as it is His. And if His waiting is nothing but goodness and graciousness, let ours be nothing but rejoicing in that goodness and confident expectation of that grace. And let every thought of waiting become for us simply the expression of pure and unspeakable blessedness, because it brings us to a God who waits so that He may make Himself perfectly known to us as the Gracious One.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: The Almighty One
fields.body_html:
Twenty-First Day. WAITING ON GOD: The Almighty One.

‘They that wait on the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with eagle wings; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.’ — Isa. 40:31.

Waiting always takes on the character of what we think of the one we are waiting on. Our waiting on God will depend greatly on what we believe Him to be. Our text comes at the end of a passage in which God reveals Himself as the Everlasting and Almighty One. It is as that revelation enters our soul that waiting will become the spontaneous expression of what we know Him to be — a God altogether worthy to be waited on.

Listen to the words: ‘Why sayest thou, O Jacob, my way is hid from the Lord?’ Why do you speak as if God does not hear or help?

‘Hast thou not known, hast thou not heard, that the Everlasting One, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?’ Far from it: ‘He giveth power to the faint, and to them that have no might He increaseth strength. Even the youths’ — ‘the glory of young men is their strength’ — ‘even the youths shall faint, and the young men shall utterly fall:’ all that people count as strong will come to nothing. ‘But they that wait on the Lord’ — on the Everlasting One, who does not faint and is not weary — they ‘shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run and,’ — listen now: they will be strong with the strength of God, and, just like Him, ‘shall not be weary; they shall walk and,’ just like Him, ‘not faint.’

Yes, ‘they shall mount up with wings as eagles.’ You know what eagles’ wings mean. The eagle is the king of birds; it soars highest into the heavens. Believers are to live a heavenly life, in the very Presence and Love and Joy of God. They are to live where God lives, and they need God’s strength to rise there. It will be given to those who wait on Him.

You know how eagles’ wings are obtained. In only one way — by being born an eagle. You are born of God. You have the eagles’ wings. You may not have known it; you may not have used them; but God can and will teach you to use them.

You know how eagles are taught to use their wings. Look at that cliff over there, rising a thousand feet out of the sea. See, high up, a ledge on the rock where there is an eagle’s nest with its treasure of two young eaglets. See the mother bird come and stir up her nest, and with her beak push the timid little birds over the edge. See how they flutter and fall and sink towards the depths. See now (Deut. 32:11) ‘how she fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings,’ and so, as they ride on her wings, carries them to a place of safety. And so she does again and again, each time throwing them out over the edge, and then catching them and carrying them once more. ‘So the Lord alone did lead him.’ Yes, the instinct of that mother eagle was God’s gift — a single ray of that love with which the Almighty trains His people to mount up as on eagles’ wings.

He stirs up your nest. He disappoints your hopes. He brings down your confidence. He makes you fear and tremble as all your strength fails and you feel utterly weary and helpless. And all the while He is spreading out His strong wings for you to rest your weakness on, and offering His everlasting Creator-strength to work in you. All He asks is that you sink down in your weariness and wait on Him, and allow Him in His Jehovah-strength to carry you as you ride on the wings of His Omnipotence.

Dear child of God, I urge you: lift up your eyes and behold your God! Listen to Him who says that He does not faint and is not weary; who promises that you too will not faint or be weary; who asks nothing but this one thing, that you should wait on Him. And let your answer be: With such a God — so mighty, so faithful, so tender —

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: Its Certainty of Blessing
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Second Day. WAITING ON GOD: Its Certainty of Blessing.

‘Thou shalt know that I am the Lord; for they shall not be ashamed that wait for Me.’ — Isa. 49:23.

‘Blessed are all they that wait for Him.’ — Isa. 30:18.

What promises! How God tries to draw us to wait on Him by the most positive assurance that it can never be in vain: ‘They shall not be ashamed that wait for Me.’ How strange it is that, though we have experienced this so often, we are still so slow to learn that this blessed waiting can and must be the very breath of our life — a continual resting in God’s presence and His love, an unceasing yielding of ourselves to Him so that He may perfect His work in us. Let us listen and meditate once again, until our heart says with new conviction: ‘Blessed are they that wait for Him!’ In our sixth day’s lesson we found the prayer in Psalm 25: ‘Let none that wait on Thee be ashamed.’ The very prayer shows how afraid we are that it might happen. Let us listen to God’s answer until every fear is driven away, and we send back to heaven the words God speaks: Yes, Lord, we believe what You say: ‘All they that wait for Me shall not be ashamed.’ ‘Blessed are all they that wait for Him.’

The context of each of these two passages points us to times when God’s Church was in great distress, and to human eyes there was no possibility of deliverance. But God steps in with His word of promise, and pledges His Almighty Power to deliver His people. And it is as the God who has Himself taken on the work of their redemption that He invites them to wait on Him, and assures them that disappointment is impossible. We, too, are living in days when there is much in the state of the Church — with its profession and its formalism — that is indescribably sad. fields.title: For Unlooked-for Things
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Third Day. WAITING ON GOD: For Unlooked-for Things.

‘For since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside Thee, what He hath prepared for him that waiteth for Him.’ — Isa. 64:4.

The R.V. reads: ‘Neither hath the eye seen a God beside Thee, which worketh for him that waiteth for Him.’ In the A.V. the thought is that no eye has seen the thing God has prepared. In the R.V., no eye has seen any God besides our God who works for the one who waits for Him. Two thoughts are common to both: that our place is to wait upon God, and that something will be revealed to us which the human heart cannot imagine. The difference is that in the R.V. it is the God who works, while in the A.V. it is the thing He is to work. In 1 Cor. 2:9 the verse is quoted of the things the Holy Spirit is to reveal, as in the A.V., and in this meditation we keep to that.

The preceding verses, especially from chapter 63:15 onwards, speak of the low condition of God’s people. The prayer has been poured out: ‘Look down from heaven.’ (ver. 15.) ‘Why hast Thou hardened my heart from Thy fear? Return for Thy servants’ sake.’ (ver. 17.) And in 64:1, more urgently still: ‘Oh that Thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, . . . as when the melting fire burneth, to make Thy name known to Thy adversaries!’ Then comes the plea from the past: ‘When Thou didst terrible things we looked not for, Thou camest down, the mountains flowed down at Thy presence.’ ‘For’ — and this is the faith awakened by the thought of the things they had not looked for: He is still the same God — ‘eye hath not seen beside Thee, O God, what He hath prepared for him that waiteth for Him.’ God alone knows what He can do for His waiting people. As Paul explains and applies it: ‘The things of God knoweth no man, save the Spirit of God.’ ‘But God hath revealed them to us by His Spirit.’

The need of God’s people, and the call for God to step in, is as urgent in our day as it was in Isaiah’s time. Now, as then — as at all times — there is a remnant who seek God with their whole heart. But if we look at Christendom as a whole, at the state of the Church of Christ, there is every reason to plead with God to tear open the heavens and come down. Nothing but a special intervention of Almighty Power will do. I fear we have no true idea of what the so-called Christian world is in God’s sight. Unless God comes down ‘as the melting fire burneth, to make known His name to His adversaries,’ our labours are comparatively fruitless. Look at the ministry — how much of it rests on human wisdom and literary culture, how little on the demonstration of the Spirit and of power. Think of the unity of the body — how little we see of the power of a heavenly love binding God’s children into one. Think of holiness — the holiness of Christlike humility and of being crucified to the world — how little the world sees that it has people among it who live in Christ in heaven, and in whom Christ and heaven live.

What is to be done? There is only one thing. We must wait upon God. And for what? We must cry, with a cry that never rests, ‘Oh that Thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might flow down at Thy presence.’ We must desire and believe, ask and expect, that God will do things we have not looked for. We must set our faith on a God of whom people do not know what He has prepared for those who wait for Him. The wonder-working God, who can go beyond all our expectations, must be the God of our confidence.

Yes, let God’s people enlarge their hearts to wait on a God who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we can ask or think. Let us join together as His chosen ones who cry to Him day and night for things no one has seen. He is able to arise and make His people a name and a praise in the earth. ‘He will wait, that He may be gracious unto you; blessed are all they that wait for Him.’

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: To Know His Goodness
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Fourth Day. WAITING ON GOD: To Know His Goodness.

‘The Lord is good unto them that wait for Him.’ — Lam. 3:25

‘There is none good but God.’ ‘His goodness is in the heavens.’ ‘Oh how great is Thy goodness, which Thou hast laid up for them that fear Thee’ ‘Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good!’ And here is the true way to enter into this goodness of God and rejoice in it: waiting upon Him. The Lord is good — yet even His children often do not know it, because they do not wait quietly for Him to reveal it. But for those who persevere in waiting, whose souls really wait, it will come true. You might think that those who have to wait are exactly the ones who might doubt it. But that only happens when they stop waiting and grow impatient. Those who truly wait will all have to say, ‘The Lord is good to them that wait for Him.’ Would you know the goodness of God fully? Then give yourself more than ever to a life of waiting on Him.

When we first enter the school of waiting upon God, our heart is set mainly on the blessings we are waiting for. God graciously uses our need and our desire for help to train us for something higher than we had in mind. We were looking for gifts; He, the Giver, longs to give Himself and to satisfy the soul with His goodness. It is for exactly this reason that He often holds back the gifts, and that the time of waiting is made so long. All the while He is seeking to win His child’s heart for Himself. He wants us not only to say, when He gives the gift, How good God is! — but, long before it comes, and even if it never comes, to be experiencing all the time: ‘It is good that a man should quietly wait’; ‘The Lord is good to them that wait for Him.’

What a blessed life the life of waiting then becomes — the continual worship of faith, adoring and trusting His goodness. As the soul learns its secret, every act of waiting simply becomes a quiet entering into the goodness of God, letting it do its blessed work and satisfy our every need. And every experience of God’s goodness makes the work of waiting more attractive. Instead of only taking refuge in God in times of need, we come to long greatly to wait on Him continually, all day long. And however much our duties and engagements fill our time and our minds, the soul grows more familiar with the secret art of always waiting. Waiting becomes the habit and the disposition of the soul — its very second nature and breath.

Dear Christian, do you not begin to see that waiting is not just one among a number of Christian virtues, to be thought of from time to time, but that it expresses the attitude that lies at the very root of the Christian life? It gives a higher value and a new power to our prayer and worship, to our faith and surrender, because it links us, in unchanging dependence, to God Himself. And it gives us the unbroken enjoyment of God’s goodness: ‘The Lord is good to them that wait for Him.’

Let me urge you once again to take the time and trouble to cultivate this much-needed element of the Christian life. We get too much of our religion second-hand, from human teaching. That teaching is of great value if it leads us to God Himself — just as John the Baptist’s preaching sent his disciples away from himself to the Living Christ. What our religion needs is more of God. Many of us are too taken up with our work. As with Martha, the very service we want to give the Master separates us from Him; it is neither pleasing to Him nor profitable to us. The more work we have, the more we need to wait upon God. Then doing God’s will, instead of exhausting us, would be our food and drink — our nourishment, refreshment and strength. ‘The Lord is good to them that wait for Him.’ How good, no one can tell except those who prove it by waiting on Him. How good, no one can fully tell except those who have proved Him to the utmost.

fields.title: Quietly
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Fifth Day. WAITING ON THE LORD: Quietly.

‘It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.’ — Lam. 3:26

‘Take heed, and be quiet: fear not, neither be faint-hearted.’ ‘In quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.’ Words like these show us the close connection between quietness and faith, and how deeply we need quietness as part of true waiting upon God. If our whole heart is to be turned towards God, it must be turned away from the creature — from everything that occupies and interests us, whether in joy or in sorrow.

God is a Being of such infinite greatness and glory, and our nature has become so estranged from Him, that it takes our whole heart and all our desires set on Him to know Him and receive Him even in some small measure. Everything that is not God — whatever stirs our fears, or prompts our efforts, or awakens our hopes, or makes us glad — hinders our perfect waiting on Him. The message is one of deep meaning: ‘Take heed and be quiet;’ ‘In quietness shall be your strength;’ ‘It is good that a man should quietly wait.’

Scripture bears abundant witness to how the very thought of God in His majesty and holiness should silence us.

‘The Lord is in His holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before Him’ (Hab. 2:20).

‘Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord God.’ (Zeph. 1:7).

‘Be silent, O all flesh, before the Lord; for He is raised up out of His holy habitation’ (Zech. 2:13).

As long as waiting on God is seen mainly as a means to more effective prayer and to getting what we ask for, this spirit of perfect quietness will not be reached. But when we see that waiting on God is itself an unspeakable blessedness — one of the highest forms of fellowship with the Holy One — then adoring Him in His glory will necessarily humble the soul into a holy stillness, making room for God to speak and reveal Himself. Then the precious promise is fulfilled that all of self and self-effort will be humbled: ‘The haughtiness of man shall be brought down, and the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.’

Let everyone who wants to learn the art of waiting on God remember the lesson: ‘Take heed, and be quiet;’ ‘It is good that a man quietly wait.’ Take time to be apart from all friends and all duties, all cares and all joys — time to be still and quiet before God. Take time to find stillness not only from people and the world, but from self and its energy. Let the Word and prayer be very precious to you; but remember that even these may get in the way of quiet waiting. The activity of the mind in studying the Word, or in putting its thoughts into words in prayer, and the activity of the heart with its desires and hopes and fears, may so absorb us that we never come to still waiting on the All-Glorious One; our whole being is not bowed down in silence before Him. At first it may seem hard to know how to wait quietly like this, with the activity of mind and heart hushed for a while. But every effort towards it will be rewarded. We will find that it grows on us, and the short time of silent worship will bring a peace and a rest that bless us not only in prayer but all day long.

‘It is good that a man should quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord.’ Yes, it is good. The quietness is a confession of our helplessness: with all our willing and running, with all our thinking and praying, it will not be done — we must receive it from God. It is a confession of our trust that our God will come to our help in His own time — a quiet resting in Him alone. It is a confession of our desire to sink into our own nothingness and to let Him work and reveal Himself. Do let us wait quietly. In daily life, let the soul that is waiting for the great God to do His wonderful work keep a quiet reverence, and a constant watch against becoming too absorbed in the world. Then the whole character will come to bear this beautiful stamp: quietly waiting for the salvation of God.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: In Holy Expectancy
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Sixth Day. WAITING ON GOD: In Holy Expectancy.

‘Therefore will I look to the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me.’ — Micah 7:7.

Have you ever read a beautiful little book called Expectation Corner? If not, get it; you will find in it one of the best sermons on our text. It tells of a king who prepared a city for some of his poor subjects. Not far away were large storehouses, from which everything they could need was supplied, if they simply sent in their requests. But there was one condition: they were to be on the lookout for the answer, so that when the king’s messengers came with the gifts they had asked for, they would always be found waiting and ready to receive them. The sad story is told of one discouraged man who never expected to get what he asked for, because he felt too unworthy. fields.title: For Redemption
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Seventh Day. WAITING ON GOD: For Redemption.

‘Simeon was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Ghost was upon him. Anna, a prophetess, . . . spake of Him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.’ — Luke 2:25, 38.

Here we have the marks of a waiting believer. Just — righteous in all his conduct. Devout — devoted to God, always walking as in His presence. Waiting for the consolation of Israel — looking for God’s promises to be fulfilled. And the Holy Ghost was on him. In his devout waiting he had been prepared for the blessing. And Simeon was not the only one. Anna spoke to all who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem. This was the one distinguishing mark of a godly group of men and women in Jerusalem, amid the formalism and worldliness all around: they were waiting on God, looking for His promised redemption.

And now that the Consolation of Israel has come, and redemption has been accomplished, do we still need to wait? We certainly do. But will our waiting — we who look back on it as having come — not be very different from the waiting of those who looked forward to its coming? It will, especially in two respects. We now wait on God in the full power of the redemption, and we wait for its full revelation.

Our waiting is now in the full power of the redemption. Christ said, ‘In that day you shall know that you are in Me. Abide in Me.’ The Epistles teach us to present ourselves to God ‘as indeed dead to sin, and alive to God in Christ Jesus,’ ‘blessed with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ Jesus.’ Our waiting on God may now be filled with the wonderful awareness — produced and kept alive by the Holy Spirit within us — that we are accepted in the Beloved; that the love that rests on Him rests on us; that we are living in that love, in the very nearness and presence and sight of God. The saints of old took their stand on the word of God and waited, hoping in that word. We rest on the word too — but, oh, with far greater privileges, as one with Christ Jesus! As we wait on God, let this be our confidence: in Christ we have access to the Father. How sure, then, we may be that our waiting cannot be in vain.

Our waiting also differs in this: they waited for a redemption still to come, while we see it accomplished and now wait for it to be revealed in us. Christ said not only, Abide in Me, but also, I in you. The Epistles speak not only of our being in Christ but of Christ in us, as the highest mystery of redeeming love. As we keep our place in Christ day by day, God waits to reveal Christ in us in such a way that He is formed in us — that His mind and disposition and likeness take on shape and substance in us — so that each one of us can truly say, ‘Christ liveth in me.’

My life in Christ up there in heaven, and Christ’s life in me down here on earth — these two complete each other. The more my waiting on God is marked by the living faith that I am in Christ, the more my heart thirsts for, and claims, CHRIST IN ME. And the waiting on God that began with particular needs and prayers will become more and more focused — as far as our personal life is concerned — on this one thing: Lord, reveal Your redemption fully in me; let Christ live in me.

Our waiting differs from that of the saints of old in the position we take and the expectations we hold. But at its root it is the same: waiting on God, from whom alone our expectation comes.

Learn one lesson from Simeon and Anna. How utterly impossible it was for them to do anything towards the great redemption — towards Christ’s birth or His death. It was God’s work. They could do nothing but wait. Are we just as completely helpless when it comes to the revelation of Christ in us? We certainly are. God did not work out the great redemption in Christ as a whole and then leave it to us to apply it in detail.

The secret thought that He did lies at the root of all our weakness. The revelation of Christ in every individual believer — and in each one, the daily revelation, step by step and moment by moment — is as much the work of God’s almighty power as the birth or resurrection of Christ. Until this truth enters and fills us, and we feel that we are just as dependent on God for every moment of our life in the enjoyment of redemption as they were in their waiting for it, our waiting upon God will not bring its full blessing. A sense of utter and absolute helplessness, and the confidence that God can and will do everything — these must be the marks of our waiting, as they were of theirs. As gloriously as God proved Himself to them to be the faithful and wonder-working God, He will prove Himself to us too.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For the Coming of His Son
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Eighth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For the Coming of His Son.

‘Be ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their Lord.’ — Luke 12:36.

‘Until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which, in His own time, He shall shew, who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords.’ — 1 Tim. 6:14, 15 (R.V.).

‘Turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for His Son from heaven.’ — 1 Thess. 1:9, 10.

Waiting on God in heaven, and waiting for His Son from heaven — God has joined these two together, and no one may separate them. Waiting on God for His presence and power in daily life is the only true preparation for waiting for Christ in humility and true holiness. Waiting for Christ to come from heaven to take us to heaven gives our waiting on God its true note of hope and joy. The Father who will reveal His Son from heaven in His own time is the God who, as we wait on Him, prepares us for that revelation of His Son. The present life and the coming glory are inseparably connected, both in God and in us.

There is sometimes a danger of separating them. It is always easier to be busy with the religion of the past or of the future than to be faithful in the religion of today. As we look at what God has done in the past, or will do in time to come, we may escape the personal claim of present duty and of present submission to His working. Waiting on God must always lead to waiting for Christ as the glorious completion of His work; and waiting for Christ must always remind us of our duty to wait upon God, as the only proof that our waiting for Christ is in spirit and in truth. There is such a danger of being taken up with the things that are coming more than with Him who is coming! The study of future events gives so much room for imagination and reason and human cleverness that nothing but a deeply humble waiting on God can save us from mistaking the interest and pleasure of intellectual study for true love of Him and of His appearing. All of you who say you are waiting for Christ’s coming, make sure that you are waiting on God now. All of you who are seeking to wait on God now to reveal His Son in you, see to it that you do so as people waiting for the revelation of His Son from heaven. The hope of that glorious appearing will strengthen you as you wait on God for what He is to do in you now. The same almighty love that will reveal that glory is working in you even now to make you ready for it.

‘The blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ’ is one of the great bonds of unity given to God’s Church throughout the ages. ‘He shall come to be glorified in His saints, and to be marveled at in all them that believe.’ Then we will all meet, and the unity of the body of Christ will be seen in its divine glory. It will be the meeting place and the triumph of divine love: Jesus receiving His own and presenting them to the Father; His own meeting Him and worshipping that blessed face in speechless love; His own meeting one another in the ecstasy of God’s own love. Let us wait for, long for and love the appearing of our Lord and Heavenly Bridegroom. Tender love for Him and tender love for one another is the true and only bridal spirit.

I greatly fear that this is sometimes forgotten. A dear brother in Holland was speaking of the expectancy of faith as the true sign of the bride. I ventured to express a doubt. An unworthy bride about to marry a prince might be thinking only of the position and riches she was going to receive. The expectancy of faith might be strong while true love was entirely missing. It is love that makes the bridal spirit. It is not when we are most taken up with prophetic subjects, but when we are clinging closely, in humility and love, to our Lord and to His brothers and sisters, that we are in the bride’s place. Jesus refuses to accept our love unless it is also love for His disciples. Waiting for His coming means waiting for the glorious future display of the unity of the body, while here and now we seek to keep that unity in humility and love. Those who love most are most ready for His coming. Love for one another is the life and beauty of His bride, the Church.

And how is this to come about? Beloved child of God, if you want to learn rightly how to wait for His Son from heaven, live even now waiting on God in heaven. Remember how Jesus lived always waiting on God. He could do nothing by Himself. It was God who perfected His Son through suffering and then exalted Him. Only God can give you the deep spiritual life of someone who is truly waiting for His Son: wait on God for it. Waiting for Christ Himself is, oh, so different from waiting for things that may happen! Any Christian can do the second; the first, God must work in you every day by His Holy Spirit. So all of you who wait on God, look to Him for grace to wait for His Son from heaven in the Spirit who is from heaven. And you who want to wait for His Son, wait on God continually to reveal Christ in you.

The revelation of Christ in us, as it is given to those who wait upon God, is the true preparation for the full revelation of Christ in glory.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God!’

fields.title: For the Promise of the Father
fields.body_html:
Twenty-Ninth Day. WAITING ON GOD: For the Promise of the Father.

‘He charged them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father.’ — Acts 1:4.

When we spoke of the saints in Jerusalem at Christ’s birth, with Simeon and Anna, we saw that although the redemption they waited for has come, the call to wait is no less urgent now than it was then. We wait for the full revelation in us of what came to them, but which they could hardly understand. It is the same with waiting for the promise of the Father. In one sense, its fulfilment can never come again as it came at Pentecost. In another sense — and that as truly and deeply as with the first disciples — we need every day to wait for the Father to fulfil His promise in us.

The Holy Spirit is not a person distinct from the Father in the way two persons on earth are distinct. The Father and the Spirit are never without each other or apart from each other. The Father is always in the Spirit; the Spirit does nothing except as the Father works in Him. At every moment the same Spirit who is in us is in God too. And the person who is most full of the Spirit will be the first to wait on God most earnestly, for Him to fulfil His promise further and to strengthen him still more mightily by His Spirit in the inner man. The Spirit in us is not a power at our disposal. Nor is the Spirit an independent power, acting apart from the Father and the Son. The Spirit is the real, living presence and power of the Father working in us. And so it is precisely the one who knows that the Spirit is in him who will wait on the Father for the full revelation and experience of what the Spirit’s indwelling means — for His increase, and for His abounding more and more.

See this in the apostles. They were filled with the Spirit at Pentecost. Not long afterwards, returning from the Council where they had been forbidden to preach, they prayed again for boldness to speak in His name — and a fresh coming down of the Holy Spirit was the Father’s fresh fulfilment of His promise.

At Samaria many had been converted through the word and the Spirit, and the whole city was filled with joy. At the apostles’ prayer the Father fulfilled the promise once again. So it was, too, for the waiting company in Cornelius’ house — ‘We are all here before God.’ And so again in Acts 13: it was when men already filled with the Spirit prayed and fasted that the promise of the Father was fulfilled afresh, and the Spirit’s leading was given from heaven: ‘Separate Me Barnabas and Saul.’

So too we find Paul in Ephesians praying for those who had been sealed with the Spirit, that God would give them the spirit of illumination; and later on, that He would grant them, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with might by the Spirit in the inner man.

The Spirit given at Pentecost was not something God parted with in heaven and sent away out of heaven to earth. God does not — cannot — give anything away in that manner. When He gives grace, or strength, or life, He gives it by giving Himself to work it; it is all inseparable from Himself. (See note on Law, The Power of the Spirit, at the end of this volume.) How much more is this true of the Holy Spirit! He is God, present and working in us. The true position in which we can count on that working with unceasing power is this: while we praise God for what we have, we still wait unceasingly for the Father’s promise to be fulfilled still more mightily.

What new meaning and promise this gives to our life of waiting! It teaches us always to keep the place where the disciples waited, at the footstool of the Throne. It reminds us that, just as they were helpless to face their enemies or to preach to Christ’s enemies until they were clothed with power, we too can only be strong in the life of faith or the work of love as we are in direct communion with God and Christ, and as they maintain the life of the Spirit in us. It assures us that the Almighty God will, through the glorified Christ, work in us a power that can bring about things unexpected — things impossible. Oh, what will the Church not be able to do when her individual members learn to live their lives waiting on God; and when together, with all of self and the world sacrificed in the fire of love, they unite in waiting with one accord for the promise of the Father — once so gloriously fulfilled, but still not exhausted!

Come, let each of us be still in the presence of the unimaginable grandeur of this prospect: the Father waiting to fill the Church with the Holy Ghost. And let each one say: He is willing to fill me.

With this faith, let a hush and a holy fear come over the soul as it waits in stillness to take it all in. And let life become more and more a deep joy in the hope of the ever fuller fulfilment of the Father’s promise.

And the person who is most full of the Spirit will be the first to wait on God most earnestly, for Him to fulfil His promise further and to strengthen him still more mightily by His Spirit in the inner man. The Spirit in us is not a power at our disposal. Nor is the Spirit an independent power, acting apart from the Father and the Son. The Spirit is the real, living presence and power of the Father working in us. And so it is precisely the one who knows that the Spirit is in him who will wait on the Father for the full revelation and experience of what the Spirit’s indwelling means — for His increase, and for His abounding more and more. At Samaria many had been converted through the word and the Spirit, and the whole city was filled with joy. At the apostles’ prayer the Father fulfilled the promise once again. So it was, too, for the waiting company in Cornelius’ house — ‘We are all here before God.’ And so again in Acts 13: it was when men already filled with the Spirit prayed and fasted that the promise of the Father was fulfilled afresh, and the Spirit’s leading was given from heaven: ‘Separate Me Barnabas and Saul.’ So too we find Paul in Ephesians praying for those who had been sealed with the Spirit, that God would give them the spirit of illumination; and later on, that He would grant them, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with might by the Spirit in the inner man. The Spirit given at Pentecost was not something God parted with in heaven and sent away out of heaven to earth. God does not — cannot — give anything away in that manner. When He gives grace, or strength, or life, He gives it by giving Himself to work it; it is all inseparable from Himself. (See note on Law, The Power of the Spirit, at the end of this volume.) fields.title: Continually
fields.body_html:
Thirtieth Day. WAITING ON GOD: Continually.

‘Therefore turn thou to thy God: keep mercy and judgment, and wait on thy God continually.’ — Hos. 12:6.

Continuity is one of the essential elements of life. Interrupt it in a person for a single hour, and life is lost; he is dead. Continuity — unbroken and unceasing — is essential to a healthy Christian life. God wants me to be, and God waits to make me — and I want to be, and I wait on Him to make me — every moment what He expects of me and what is pleasing in His sight. If waiting on God is of the essence of true religion, then the spirit of complete dependence must be kept up continually. God’s call, ‘Wait on your God continually,’ must be accepted and obeyed. There may be times of special waiting; but the disposition and habit of the soul must be there, unchanging and uninterrupted.

This waiting continually is in fact a necessity. To those who are content with a weak Christian life it seems a luxury, something beyond what is needed to be a good Christian. But all who are praying the prayer, ‘Lord, make me as holy as a pardoned sinner can be made! Keep me as near to You as it is possible for me to be! Fill me as full of Your love as You are willing to!’ feel at once that it is something they must have. They feel that there can be no unbroken fellowship with God, no full abiding in Christ, no lasting victory over sin and readiness for service, without waiting continually on the Lord.

Waiting continually is a possibility. Many think it is out of the question with all the duties of life. They cannot always be thinking about it; even when they want to, they forget.

They do not understand that it is a matter of the heart, and that whatever fills the heart occupies it even when the thoughts are busy with other things. A father’s heart may be continually filled with intense love and longing for a sick wife or child far away, even while urgent business takes up all his thoughts. When the heart has learned how utterly powerless it is to keep itself for a single moment or to produce any good; when it has understood how surely and truly God will keep it; when, despairing of itself, it has accepted God’s promise to do the impossible for it — then it learns to rest in God, and in the midst of work and temptation it can wait continually.

This waiting is a promise. God’s commands are enablings; the precepts of the gospel are all promises, a revelation of what our God will do for us. When you first begin to wait on God, it will be with many breaks and many failures. But do believe that God is watching over you in love and secretly strengthening you in it. There are times when waiting seems like simply wasting time, but it is not. Waiting, even in darkness, is progress you are not aware of, because it is God you are dealing with, and He is working in you. God, who calls you to wait on Him, sees your weak efforts and works the waiting in you. Your spiritual life is in no way your own work. You can no more continue it than you could begin it. It is God’s Spirit who has begun in you the work of waiting upon God, and He will enable you to wait continually.

Waiting continually will be met and rewarded by God Himself working continually. We are coming to the end of our meditations. If only you and I might learn one lesson: God must, and God will, work continually. He always does work continually, but our experience of it is hindered by unbelief. But He who by His Spirit teaches you to wait continually will also bring you to experience that, as the Everlasting One, His work never ceases. In the love and the life and the work of God there can be no break, no interruption.

Do not limit God in this by your own ideas of what may be expected. Fix your eyes on this one truth: by His very nature God, as the only Giver of life, cannot do anything other than work in His child every moment. Do not look only at one side: ‘If I wait continually, God will work continually.’ No, look at the other side. Put God first and say, ‘God works continually; every moment I may wait on Him continually.’ Take time, until the vision of your God working continually, without a moment’s pause, fills your being. Your waiting continually will then come of itself. Full of trust and joy, the holy habit of the soul will be: ‘On Thee do I wait all the day.’ The Holy Spirit will keep you always waiting.

fields.title: Moment by Moment
fields.body_html:
MOMENT BY MOMENT

‘I the Lord do keep it: I will water it every moment.’

Dying with Jesus, by death reckoned mine,

Living with Jesus a new life divine;

Looking to Jesus till glory doth shine,

Moment by moment, O Lord, I am Thine.

Chorus—Moment by moment I'm kept in His love,

Moment by moment I've life from above;

Looking to Jesus till glory doth shine;

Moment by moment, O Lord, I am Thine.

Never a battle with wrong for the right,

Never a contest that He doth not fight;

Lifting above us His banner so white,

Moment by moment I'm kept in His sight.

Chorus.

Never a trial that He is not there,

Never a burden that He doth not bear,

Never a sorrow that He does not share,

Moment by moment I'm under His care.

Chorus

Never a heartache, and never a groan,

Never a teardrop, and never a moan;

Never a danger but there on the throne

Moment by moment He thinks of His own.

Chorus.

Never a weakness that He doth not feel,

Never a sickness that He cannot heal;

Moment by moment, in woe or in weal,

Jesus, my Savior, abides with me still.

Chorus.

(Music in Christian Endeavor Hymns by I. D. Sankey). Or on leaflet by Morgan & Scott

fields.title: Only
fields.body_html:
Thirty-First Day. WAITING ON GOD: Only.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God;

For my expectation is from Him.

He only is my rock and my salvation.’ — Ps. 62:5, 6.

It is possible to be waiting on God continually, but not only on Him. Other secret confidences may come in between and keep away the blessing we were expecting. And so the word only must come and shed its light on the path to the fullness and certainty of blessing. ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God. He only is my Rock.’

Yes, ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ There is only one God, only one source of life and happiness for the heart. He only is my Rock; my soul, wait only on Him. You want to be good? ‘There is none good but God,’ and there is no goodness possible except what is received directly from Him. You have tried to be holy? ‘There is none holy but the Lord,’ and there is no holiness except what He breathes into you every moment by His Spirit of holiness. You want to live and work for God and His kingdom, for people and their salvation? Hear what He says: ‘The Everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He “alone” fainteth not, neither is weary. He giveth power to the faint, and to them that have no might He increaseth strength. They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength.’ He only is God; He only is your Rock: ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ You will not find many who can help you in this. There will be plenty of your fellow believers to draw you into putting your trust in churches and doctrines, in schemes and plans and human methods, in the means of grace and divine ordinances. But: ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God Himself.’ Even His most sacred ordinances become a snare when we put our trust in them. The bronze serpent became Nehushtan; the ark and the temple became a vain confidence. Let the Living God alone — no one and nothing but Him — be your hope.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ Eyes and hands and feet, mind and thought, may have to be fully occupied with the duties of this life; still, ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ You are an immortal spirit, created not for this world but for eternity and for God. O my soul, grasp your destiny! Know your privilege, and ‘wait thou only upon God.’ Do not let the interest of religious thoughts and exercises deceive you; very often they take the place of waiting upon God. My soul, wait — you, your very self, your innermost being, with all its powers — ‘wait thou only upon God.’ God is for you, and you are for God; wait only on Him.

Yes, ‘my soul, wait thou only upon God.’ Beware of your two great enemies — the World and Self. Beware that no earthly satisfaction or enjoyment, however innocent it seems, keeps you from saying, ‘I will go to God, my exceeding joy.’ Remember and study what Jesus says about denying self: ‘Let a man deny himself.’ Tersteegen says: ‘The saints deny themselves in everything.’ Pleasing self in little things may be strengthening it to assert itself in greater things. ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God;’ let Him be all your salvation and all your desire. Say continually, and with an undivided heart, ‘From Him comes my expectation; He only is my Rock; I shall not be moved.’ Whatever your spiritual or earthly need, whatever the desire or prayer of your heart, whatever your concern for God’s work in the Church or in the world — whether alone or in the rush of the world, in public worship or in other gatherings of the saints — ‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ Let your expectations come from Him alone. He only is your Rock.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ Never forget the two foundation truths on which this blessed waiting rests. If you are ever inclined to think that this ‘waiting only’ is too hard or too high, they will call you back at once. They are: your absolute helplessness, and the absolute sufficiency of your God. Oh, enter deeply into the complete sinfulness of everything that comes from self, and do not think of letting self have any say for a single moment. Enter deeply into your utter and unceasing powerlessness ever to change what is evil in you, or to produce anything spiritually good. Enter deeply into your relationship of dependence, as a creature, on God, receiving from Him every moment what He gives. Enter more deeply still into His covenant of redemption, with His promise to restore, more gloriously than ever, what you had lost, and by His Son and Spirit to give you within, unceasingly, His actual divine Presence and Power. And so wait upon your God continually, and only on Him.

‘My soul, wait thou only upon God.’ No words can tell, no heart can imagine, the riches of the glory of this mystery of the Father and of Christ. Our God, in the infinite tenderness and almighty power of His love, is waiting to be our Life and Joy. Oh, my soul, let there be no more need for me to repeat the words ‘Wait upon God’; but let all that is within me rise up and sing: ‘Truly my soul waits upon God. On Thee do I wait all the day.’

fields.title: Note
fields.body_html:
NOTE.

My publishers have just issued a work by William Law on the Holy Spirit. [The Power of the Holy Spirit: An humble earnest, and affectionate Address to the Clergy. With Additional Extracts and Introduction, by Rev. Andrew Murray. (Fleming H. Revell Company. $1.00)] In the Introduction I have said how much I owe to this book. I cannot help thinking that anyone who takes the trouble to read it thoughtfully will find rich spiritual profit for a life of Waiting upon God.

What he puts more clearly than I have found anywhere else are these cardinal truths:

1. That the very Nature and Being of God, as the only Possessor and Giver of whatever life there is in the universe, means that He must every moment impart to every creature the power by which it exists — and therefore, much more, the power by which it can do what is good.

2. That the very Nature and Being of a creature, which owes its existence to God alone and owes Him, just as much, the continuation of that existence every moment, means that its happiness can only be found in absolute, unceasing, moment-by-moment dependence on God.

3. That the great value and blessing of the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost, as the fruit of Christ’s Redemption, is that it is now possible for God to take possession of His redeemed children and work in them as He did in Adam before the fall. We need to know the Holy Spirit as the Presence and Power of God in us, restored to their true place.

4. That in the spiritual life our great need is to know two great lessons. The first is our complete sinfulness and helplessness — our utter inability, by any effort of our own, to do anything towards maintaining and increasing our inner spiritual life. The second is the infinite willingness of God’s love, which is nothing but a desire to share Himself and His blessedness with us, to meet our every need, and every moment to work in us by His Son and Spirit what we need.

5. That therefore the very essence of true religion, whether in heaven or on earth, consists in an unchanging dependence on God. For we can give God no other glory than to yield ourselves to His love, which created us to display its glory in us, so that it may now perfect its work in us.

I need not point out how deeply these truths go to the very root of the spiritual life, and especially of the life of waiting upon God. I am confident that those who are willing to take the trouble to study this thoughtful writer will thank me for introducing them to his book. The book referred to is The Power of the Spirit, by William Law, An Humble, Earnest and Affectionate Address to the Clergy.
